summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family '. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum representing the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals, but the High Court, following its earlier decision in Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax, A.P., held that the assessee was liable to be included in wealth tax assessments of the assessee. Dismissing the appeals by the Revenue, this Court, HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on any valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate value. of all the debts owed by the assessee on that valuation date. " The definition of "valuation date" in section 2(q) of the Act indicates that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last day of the "previous year" as the valuation date. [310B C] 2. The system of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets of the assessee.[310C] 3. The assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounting adopted by the assessee. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Wealth tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date.[310D E] 4. The assets of the respondent assessee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be consider ed are not circumscribed, by any consideration, of the particular method of accounting adopted, by the assessee.[309E] 5. The assets in the instant case are not confined only to cash. What accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets of an assessee under the Wealth Tax. [310F] Vedreva Venkatappa Rao vs C.I.T., A.P. and Commissioner of Wealth tax vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju, , approved. Commissioner of Wealthtax, A. P. I vs Pachigolla Narasimha Rao, , overruled.

The respondent was a clerk in the appellant 's project. He was charge sheeted for defi nition of the project. The inquiry was held by the Inquiry Officer. The report of the Inquiry Officer was forwarded to the competent authority who after giving an opportunity of being heard dismissed the respondent from service. The respondent moved the Central Administrative Tribunal which held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty imposed by the competent authority on the ground that it was excessive or disproportionate to the misconduct proved. The Tribunal remitted the matter to the Government for fresh considera tion for a proper punishment. The Tribunal, however, held that the penalty imposed was not commensurate with the delinquency of the respondent. The High Court, in appeal, upheld the order of the Tribunal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal could not interfere with the penal ty awarded by the competent authori ty on the ground of its excessive or disproportionate t o the misconduct proved, that the Tribunal was just a substitute to the civil court and High Court, that the High Court was in error in directing the Governor of Orissa to reconsider the question, that the respondent was not entitled to any back wages, that the punishment of dismissal was disproportionate to the gravity of misdemeanour established, and that the Tribunal should have directed the re spondent to reconsider the penalty. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Tribunal to interfere with t he disciplinary matters or punishment cannot be equated with an appellate jurisdiction. The Tribunal cannot interfere with the findings of the Inquiry Offi cer or competent authority where they are not arbitrary or utterly perverse. It is appropriate to rememb er that the power to impose penalty on a delinquent officer is conferred on the competent authority either by an Act of legislature or rules made under the provi sions of the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the Tribunal has no power to substitute its own discretion for that of the authority. The adequacy of penalty unless it is malafide is not a matter for the Tribunal to concern with. The Tribu nal also cannot interfere with tire penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry officer or the competent authority is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. Ordinarily, the Tribunal or the Court can not substitute its own er own discretion for the penalty imposed. [33E G] 2. The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to impose any punishment to meet the ends of justice. There may be cases where the penalty is imposed und er clause (a) of the second proviso to Article 311(2) of the Constitution, the Tribunal may remit the matter to t he competent authority for reconsideration or to itself substitute one of the penalties provided under clause (a). A Government servant who is aggrieved by the penalty imposed can agitate in appeal, revision or review, as the case may be, that the penalty was too seve r or excessive and not warranted by the facts and circumstances of the case or the requirements of that particular government service. [33H; 34A] 3. Ordinarily, where the Court finds that the penalty i mposed by the impugned order is arbitrary or grossly excessive or out of all proportion to the offence committed or not warranted by t he facts and circumstances in the case or to the requirements of the particular government serv ice, the Court will also strike down the impugned order. [34B] 4. The Tribunal can also remit the matter if it is satisfied that the penalty is too severe or excessive and is not warranted by facts and circumstances. [34C] 5. The Tribunal also cannot interfere in the penalty if the penalty is found to he arbitrary or grossly exce sive or out of any proportion to the misdemeanor. [34D] 6. The Tribunal should also keep in mind that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the respondent was in excess of the penalty which was imposed on him by the competent au thority. [34E] 7. The Tribunal is not concerned to decide whether the punishment imposed, provided it is just by the rules, is appropriate having regard to the misdeeds established. [34F] 8. The Tribunal could not substitute its discretion for that which the authori ty had found to be in its favour. [34G]

The appellant filed a suit for possession of the suit property on the ground that he was the lawful tenant of the suit land and since he had not been dispossessed, he was liable to be evicted. The respondents contended that the suit was not maintainable and deserved to be dismissed. The trial court dismissed the suit. The first appellate court confirmed the findings of the trial court. The High Court, however, held that the suit filed by the appellant was barred by res judicata as well as Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High court held that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed the second suit, was clearly barred by res judi cata. The High, Court, therefore, held that it was not necessary to decide the second suit on merits. The High. Court, therefore. held that the decree passed by the Civil Court was unsustainable. The High Courts order was challenged by the appellant in this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Civil Court undoubtedly had jurisdiction under section 9 of the Code to try and grant eviction till the Fifth Amendment became effective. By virtue of section 7 any question whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court stood ousted by section 58(2) of the Act. The question is whether this subsequent change in the law deprived the Civil Court of jurisdiction which it undoubtedly possessed on the date of the institution of the suit. [1028C D] 1.2 The Civil Court, undoubtedly, had jurisdiction under Section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code to try an issue relating to the status of the plaintiff as a tenant. The jurisdiction is, therefore, vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 read with section 58(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 and section 58(3) specifically bars the jurisdiction of all other courts to settle, decide or deal with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [1029C D] 1032 1.3 The jurisdiction is vested in the Civil Court under section 58(i) of the Tenancy Act and section 58 (2) specifically bars that jurisdiction. [1030B] 1.4 The Civil Court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. It would be open to the Civil Court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of the agricultural land. [1031B] 1:5 The effect of the Fifth Amendment is that the Civil Court would be precluded from deciding, even incidentally, questions failing within the ambit of section 7 of the Act or section 58(ii) of the said Act or section 7 of this Act or section 9 of this Act. [1032C] 1.6 The effect of section 7 read along with section 58 (ii) of this Act is that the jurisdiction of Civil Court stands completely barred by virtue of section 58(iii) of the Maharashtra Act. [1132D] 1.7 The Civil Court will have jurisdiction to decide any question relating to the title of the plaintiff to the agricultural land and the question of the plaintiff 's tenancy in respect of the agricultural lands will have to be decided under the provisions of the Tenancy Law. [1133B] 1,8. The Civil court will have jurisdiction only to decide the question of tenancy in respect thereof. [1134C] 1:9. The Civil Judge will have jurisdiction in respect of any other question relating to title of the parties. [1135C] 1 :10. The Civil suit is not barred by res Judicata. [1136D] 1:11. The High ' Court was wrong in holding that the second suit is barred by resjudicata. [1137D] 1 :12. The High] Court was wrong on the view that the subject suit was directly barred by res Judi cata because the subject matter was directly and materially in issue in that suit. [1138E] 1:13. The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question or from any other matter which any Mamlatdar is empowered by or under this Act to decide. [1139B] 1 :14. The jurisdiction to decide the suit is expressly barred by section 58 (3) of this act. [1140C] 1;15. The Civil Procedure Code is a complete Code in itself and it is not possible to accept the contention that the Civil Procedure Codes are not applicable to the proceedings under the Act. [II11B] 1;16. The Civil Courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature of which the value does not exceed Rs.2 lakhs. [1141C] 1 ;12. The Civil courts have jurisdiction to entertain and decide suits of a civil nature of not exceeding Rs.2lakhs. [1142D] 1;13. The Civil and the Civil Courts are not Courts of Civil Jurisdiction. The Civil or the Civil Courts have no jurisdiction to decide or deal With any question or to determine any right or issue in any suit or proceeding between the parties. The Civil as well as the Civil Courts exercise concurrent jurisdiction in respect thereof and the Civil Court is precluded from deciding any question or any issue in any appeal arising under the Act or under any other law for the time being in force. [1143B C] 1 :15. The jurisdiction conferred on the Civil Court by section 9 of Civil Procedure Code, 1908 is a special jurisdiction. The Civil is a special machinery. The Civil cannot be said to have been given a special jurisdiction in respect to any of the matters in the Second Schedule. [1144C] 1,16. The jurisdiction under section 7 of Bombay Tenancy Act is not a general jurisdiction. It is a special remedy provided for the benefit of the tenant. The Civil, Court has no jurisdiction to entertain or decide any suit or proceedings between the parties to the proceedings. [1145B] 1 ;17. The Civil Suit is not barred under section 58 (iii) of this Bombay Tenancy Act. [1745C] 1

The petitioners are carpenter and craftsmen in the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the Corporation). They are being paid the same wages as are payable to carpenter, painter and carpenter in regular service. They claim payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular service, as carpentry or craftsmen ' helpers, painters and carpenters ' helpers engaged in the construction industry. They claim that they are entitled to have the same pay as carpenter or craftsman 's helpers engaged by the Corporation. The Corporation resisted the claim on the ground that the unit where the petitioners are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The Corporation has not fixed the minimum wages payable to the petitioners engaged in the Corporation or other like industries, but the Corporation has adopted the minimum wages paid to carpenterers and painters and craftsman engaged in the Construction Industry. The Corporation is a company which has been incorporated under the . The main object of the Corporation as seen from the Memorandum of Association is to preserve the traditional arts and crafts and also to popularise handicrafts and handloom items in the State of Himachal Pradesh and other parts of the country and abroad. In order to achieve this primary object, the Corporation gives training to artisans, weavers and crafts men in various traditional arts, and crafts. During the period of training, the trainees are paid a stipend by the Corporation, and upto 31st March, 1987, the Corporation has imparted training to as many as 1662 persons in different areas like carpet weaving, handloom weaving, painting, metal crafts, wood carving, etc. Apart from giving training, the Corporation also ensures marketing support to the artisans and craftsmans by purchasing their products at remunerative prices and sell them through the marketing network of the Corporation. It is said that the village artisans and the craftsmen make different items on a piece rate basis and in some cases, they execute the work in their own homes. The financial aspect of the Corporation is stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. Nonetheless, for the purpose of preserv ing and promoting traditional arts arts and Crafts, the Corporation had been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen are employed. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. The princi ple was incorporated only under Article 39(d) of the Constitution as a Directive Principle of State Policy. The Corporation, therefore, has been kept alive and is being paid the minimum wages as prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner under exhibit P. 2 dated March 20, 1986. The Corporation had also adopted the minimum wage rates in the construction sector. The Corporation was, therefore, not paying the same wages to the petitioners. The petitioners have filed this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay fo r equal work" and for regularisation of their services with the benefits of "equal wages" as applicable to the carpenter workers in the construction Industry. The petitioners claimed that they are discharging same duties and performing similar functions as those of the carpentors, painters, carpenter etc. in the Government service. The Corporation contested the petition on the ground, inter alia, that the Corporation is a Company which has been registered under the . It has been set up under the . In order to implement the provisions of the . the Corporation has been setup under the . As per the Memorandum of the Corporation, the Corporation is to be a Company registered under the Companies Act. The main object is to preserve and promote traditional arts. The Corporation gives training and the petitioners are paid stipend by it. The Corporation further contended that the village artists and crafts mentsmen make different kinds of items on a par with the carpentry workers. The Corporation also ensures that the carpress and crafts workers are not paid less than the carperers. The Corporation provides for the proper maintenance of the village arts and the craft ments. The Corporation does not employ carpentry and crafts manuscents. The petitioners are not doing any work of a permanent nature. They are not paid any minimum wages. The Corporation cannot claim to be a 'State ' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. The Corporation being a company, it has been set in motion by the State Government. The Corporation enjoys monopoly status in the field of arts and culture and crafts, and the State Government has been entrusted with the task of providing for the betterment of the arts and cultural heritage. The Corporation carries on the business of exhibiting arts and performing arts. It has been established under the . There is no regular employees of the petitioners. It is not a 'State Government '. The Corporation acts as a 'State Public Sector Undertaking '. The petitioners cannot claim wages payable to their counterparts, in government service. The petitioners were not doing any 'work of a permanent or quasi permanent nature. The Corporation 's main object is the welfare of the artists and the craftsman in the field. The Corporation pays the petitioners a fixed sum as salary. The Corporation can neither deny the petitioners nor refuse to pay the same. The Corporation may not deny the petitioners the right to continue in service. The question of regularisation of the services of the petitioners does not arise. The Corporation shall pay the petitioners the minimum wages prescribed by the State under exhibit P 2 dated March, 20, 1986, as amended from time to time. The prosecution alleged that the seven accused, who were charged with the murder of one Malan, committed the murder of her daughter and that the approver P.W. 1, the approver, was a party to the conspiracy to commit the murders of her daughter, and that the accused 1 to 3, who were also charged with the offence of conspiracy to commit murder of the deceased, committed the murders of the deceased and the approver. The Sessions Judge found on a consideration of the evidence, all the seven accused not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and acquitted them. He found accused 1 to 4 not guilty of charge No. 2 framed against them in respect of the murder of the daughter of the deceased. He found the accused 1 and 6 guilty of charge under section 302 I.P C. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life under section 302/34 I.P Act. The State did not file any appeal against the acquittal of accused 1 and 2 of charge No, 1 framed against them under section 302 IPC. As regards accused 1 and 3, the Sessions Judge found them guilty of charge section 302 read section 34 I.P .C. and sentenced each of them to imprisonment of life under section 120B IPC. The High Court dismissed the appeal of accused 1 to 6 and allowed the appeal of the State for enhancement of the sentence of imprisonment for life awarded to accused 1 and sixteen for the murder of Malan and acquitted them of the charge. The High court also acquitted accused 7 and convicted accused 1 and 5 and sentenced them under section 120 B read with section 34 I P.C. to imprisonment for three years. The State filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Court in respect of accused 1, 6 and 7. The State also filed an appeal for enhancement of sentence of imprisonment of accused 1 for the murder. The High ' Court dismissed the appeals of accused 1 6 and 7 and allowed the appeals of the State in respect of charge No 1 framed under section 120 A I.P,C. and convicted accused 6 and 7 under section 302, read with section 109 I.P 'C. The High. Court acquitted accused 7, 8 and 9 of the charge under section 120A I.P.,C. and confirmed the conviction and sentence of accused 1 under section 120, read with Section 109 I. P.C., and acquitted accused 7. The High, Court dismissed the State 's appeal against the acquittals of accused 1 8 and 9 and allowed the State ' 's appeal in respect of charges under section 120 and acquitted accused 1 and 7. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the conviction of accused 1 was unsustainable in law as at least two persons were required for an offence of conspiracy under section 120(A) I.P,.C. and he relied upon a decision of this Court in Topandas vs State of Bombay, ; , in support of his contention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge for conspiracy under section 302 r/w section 120B. The judicial confession of P.W I was not voluntary and reliable and it was not corroborated by other evidence. [782B] 3. The retracted Judicial confession of accused 6 could not be acted upon against accused 7 in view of his acquittal by the High court of the charge framed under section 109 read with section 114 I.P P.C, and the evidence of the judicial confession, Exh. 138 of accused 6 was not reliable and it could not be accepted. [783B] 4. The retracted confession of accused 7 could not be used against accused 6 as it was not voluntary. [784B] 5. The evidence against accused 6 was also not reliable. [789C] 6. The evidence regarding the recovery of the razor blade, article 54, which was recovered from the scene of offence before and after the commission of the murder, could not be believed. [781D] 7. It could not be said that the evidence relating to recovery of the body of the dead man was not reliable because it was not reliable in view of certain circumstances. [787B] 10. The evidence on record was not sufficient to prove the guilt of accused 6 for the murder and the conviction of the accused for the murder was not sustainable. [788C] 11. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the will set up by her was not genuine and was not valid and that she was entitled to make a will in respect of her properties. The respondents contested the suit on the ground that the will was not genuine, that the appellant had no title to the properties and that the will had been executed by her without understanding its nature and effect. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the trial court and decreed the suit on a finding that the will in question was genuine and valid. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to a half share in the properties in suit and that the respondents were entitled to a maintenance in respect of the properties. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. The main contention of the appellant was that the will, set up by the appellant was not genuine. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that the will did not set up a will but a will and that the appellant 's intention was to make a gift of the properties to her husband and that the testator had no intention of making a will in favour of the appellant. Held, that the will setting up a will was genuine and was valid. The testatrix was not in a sound disposing state of mind and the will was therefore valid. The will set up a disposition of the properties covered by it in favour of her husband and the appellant. The will was not unnatural and was not surrounded by suspicious circumstances. The High court was justified in reversing the finding of the trial Court on the question of due and valid execution of the will. The evidence of the witnesses examined by the appellant on the question about the execution of the document was inconsistent with the appellant ' 's case about previous instructions and so it would be difficult to treat the evidence of the witness as sufficient to prove that the testatrix fully understood the nature of the recitals in the will. Sarat Kumari Bibi vs Sakhi Chand, (1931) L.R. 55 I.A. 1, referred to. The evidence on the question as to the execution of a will was not satisfactory and sufficient to prove the sound and disposing state of the testator 's mind and his signature as required by law. The High Courts in India have consistently held that the onus probandi lies in every case upon the propounder of a will and he must satisfy the conscience of the court that the instrument so propounded is the last will of a free and capable testator. The test merely emphasizes that, in determining the question as t.o whether an instrument produced before the court is the last of the will of a testator, the court is deciding a solemn question and it must be fully satisfied that it had been validly executed by the testator who is no longer alive. It may, however, be stated generally that a propounder of the will has to prove the due and valid executed of the will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of will the propounder must remove the said suspicions from the mind of the court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. It is hardly necessary to add that the result of the application of these two general and broad principles would always depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case and on the nature and quality of the evidence adduced by the parties. The test simply emphasizes that in determining the questions as to whether an instrument is the last Will of a free, and capable testator, the Court is deciding a purely solemn question of fact and it must, therefore, be fully satisfied by the propounder that the will has been validly executed and that it was signed by the testator. The question as to whether a particular will was the last will and testament of a free testator would depend upon the intention of the testator as disclosed by the various shades of mental dispositions and habits of the testator and the dispositions made by him and the evidence led by the parties in that connection. The test only emphasizes that the will must be read as a whole and the testators signature or attestation must be proved by the propounders and it is not necessary to examine any one of the witnesses to prove the signature or attestation. The evidence as to the mental capacity of the testator to execute the will has also to be considered in the light of the surrounding circumstances. The test therefore is not an abstract test but how the testator had understood the nature and effect of his dispositions before he put his signature to the will. In the present case the testatres were clear and unambiguous and the evidence was sufficient to prove their sound and disposing of the testators mind and their signature as required under law. Sarat Kuar Bibi vsSakhi Chand, , referred to. In the instant case the evidence of P.W. 1 was not satisfactory. The evidence was inconsistent with that of the appellant ' s case about previous instruc tions and so it was not safe to rely on it. The evidence did not show satisfactorily that the will which was produced before the Court was the last of a free will of the testator. Sarat Kumar Bibi vsKeshwar Lal Bibi, (1930) L. R. 55 I A. 1, relied on. The evidence in the present case was not satisfactory as to the intention of P. W. 1. The evidence showed that the testator was not in sound disposing state and that the testators mental capacity was not such as to make the will genuine. The evidence also did not show that the testator fully understood the contents of the will before he put her signature to the document. The evidence therefore was not sufficient to prove due execution of the testat ers. The evidence that the testator signed the will after understanding its contents and that the signature of the testators was obtained by the testator after the will was written, was not sufficient. The evidence about the execution was inconsistent with his case that the testa tionators had signed the will in the presence of the testator, and the evidence that the testator signed the will without understanding its contents, was not satisfactory, as to the nature of his mental capacity. The evidence, therefore, was not adequate to prove due and valid attestation of the will by the testators. Sarat kumar Bibi vs Sankal Chand Bibi, , referred. The evidence regarding the mental capacity and the signature of P. was not satisfactory because the evidence was inconsistent and inconsistent with the evidence of appellant 's case that the testator read out the will to the testat er and that he read it out to the testator and that the latter signed it after understanding its nature. The evidence could not be accepted as sufficient to establish the due and proper attestation of the Will. The evidence relating to the mental condition of the testator was inconsistent with her case that the will read out to her was a will. The testators signature was not proved to be that of the testator but was a mere mistake. The evidence established that the testator knew that the test ant signed the will at the time of the execution of it and that he signed it after fully understanding its contents. The evidence proved that the testator put his signature on the will after fully understanding the contents of it and the evidence established that he signed the will with the intention of signing it. The testator had no intention to make a bequest to the test ant and the evidence showed that he signed in the presence and under the direction of the test ant

The appellant company manufactured cinema arc carbons. The appellant company was registered as a dealer under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant was assessed to sales tax for the assessment year 1965 66 on the ground that they fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Act. The High Court referred to the fact that the appellant had not produced their account books to show that they had been purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to claim exemption from sales tax under the entry. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the appellant company was not entitled under the entry to claim exemption. [562 B] (1) The entry No. 3 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No. 6 for "wireless reception instruments and apparatus" includes "electrical valves, accumulators, amplifiers and loud speakers and spare parts and accessories thereof". Entry No. 2, relating to refrigerators, air conditioning plants covers also "component parts thereof". Again, entry No. 5 for "wires" includes "component part and accessories thereof" and "articles (including batteries) adapted for use as parts and accessories of motor vehicles". Entry No, 3, for "wares" is used in the same sense in which it is used in entry No, 4. [563 B D] (2) The term "accessories" is used to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [563 E] (3) The High Court correctly held that the main use of the are carbons under consideration was that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. [564 B C]

The Gujarat Minor Minerals Rules, 1966 were framed under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. Rule 21 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor minerals. Rule 21 provides for the fixation of the rate at which royalty is to be charged in respect of any mineral. Rule 21(1) provides that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, fix the rate of dead rent in respect of each class of minerals. Rule 22 provides for the revision of the rate fixed by the Central Government. Rule 21A provides for the enhancement of the rate in respect of minerals other than minor minerals. The petitioners in the writ petitions who were lessees of minor minerals challenged the levy of royalty on the minor minerals in the State of Gujarat. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in the instant case was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The State of Gujarat and the Union of India contended that the levy was justified under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution and that the Act was passed for purposes of regulation and development of minerals. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The royalty levied and the cess collected under the Act are not in the nature of a fee which could be used only for specific purposes. The Act is passed for the purpose of regulation and develop ment of minerals. It is not an imposition made by a law made by the State Legislature on which alone the restriction contemplated under Article 304(b) of the Constitution applies. [413C D] 2. The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliar Community of Manjakollai village in a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the appellant the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and the affairs were always vested in the community of the Sengungars and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the temple. The appellant 's case was that the temple was declared as an "exempted" temple under the provisions of Madras Act 1 of 1925. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. The respondents filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. The appellant came to this Court by certificate. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Act. HELD: (i) The phrase "regulated" in section 6(1) of the Madras Act must be construed along with the phrase "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. The word "success" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another" (vide in Re: Hindu Women 's Right to Property Act, 1941 (1). [426 D] (ii) The word "hereditary" in relation of property and rights in Hindu Law means "the right of a person belonging to a particular religious community or the right of a group of persons belonging to a specified religious community or a specified locality to take certain property in the hands of a person professing a particular religious faith or belief. [426 H] (iii) The election to the office of trustee in the present case was for a fixed period of one years and not for life. It was, therefore, difficult to hold that the office of the appellant was hereditary within the meaning Of section 6(a) of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act. [426 G] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, [1954] S.C.R. 1005, followed. State of Madras V. Ramakrishna, ; , referred to.

The appellant was charged under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 IPC and section 302/34 IPC. The prosecution case was that the appellant and his father, who was a leper, were alleged to have inflicted injuries on the deceased with a knife. The deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space. The appellant and his brother were alleged to be armed with knives and a knife. They were alleged to hack him on the ground. The deceased got up and saw the appellant running on the eastern bank of the channel with a knife, and the electric lights were burning in the vicinity. The appellant was alleged to have run to his elder brother who was sleeping on the eastern side of the sluice. The deceased went to his younger brother and got up and found him running. He got up and went near him and saw the accused running on the western bank of the slam. The deceased had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. The appellant ran to his elder brothers and told them that he had killed the deceased. The brothers of the deceased went to the police station and lodged a report. The appellant 's brother was also examined as a witness. The appellant, however, was not examined. The appellant filed a petition of complaint against the deceased and his brother for the offence of murder. The Sessions Judge convicted the appellant and the brother of the deceased under section 302 read with section 34 IPC and section 109 IPC and sentenced them to death. The High Court acquitted the brother of murder but confirmed the conviction and sentence of death. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the testimony of the sole eye witness was not corroborated by the contents of the FIR and the testimony of PW 4, that the evidence of PW 4 was not corroborated in material particulars by the contents in the FIR and that the evidence was not sufficient to prove the guilt of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was not right in holding that the testimony was not corroborated. The testimony of the solitary eye witness was rejected by the Sessions Judge on the ground that he was wholly unreliable. The High 'Court was not right that PW 4 stood wholly corroborated by the FIR. The testimony was not sufficient for the conviction of the appellant and sentence of capital punishment was set aside. [711D E] 2. The High Courts should not ordinarily interfere with the findings of the trial court in a murder case. The High courts should not have taken a view of the evidence of the sole witness without considering the intrinsic quality of the evidence. [712B C] 3. The High, Court was not right and the conviction and sentences of death were set aside. The appellant shall be released forthwith. [713C]

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of a deceased person. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. The respondents contended that the amounts received by the heirs and the legal representatives of the deceased were not the income of the deceased and were not liable to tax under section 24B(1) of the Income tax Act. The respondents relied on the scheme of the Act as given in Additional Income tax Officer vs E. Alfred, and on certain observations in Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay, ; , and contended that the income received subsequent to the previous year in which the deceased died was liable to be assessed to income tax under section 23(4) of the Act. Held, that the income which was received subsequent to its death was liable to tax as income in the hands of the heirs and was not liable to be taxed in the hands Of the heirs and their legal representatives. The fiction in section 24B does not extend to tax liability of the estate of a deceased assessee beyond the previous or the account year in which that person died. In the present case the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable to. be taxed in. the several years of assessment. Ellis vs Trehearne, , applied. Elliis C. R. vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, , referred to. The individual assessee has ordinarily to be a living person and there can be no assessment on a dead person and the assessment is a charge in respect of the income of a previous year and not a charge in regard to the income of that year as measured by the income of previous year. Wallace Brothers & Co. Ltd. vs Commissioner Of Income tax, , referred. The individual assesses have ordinarily to be living persons and there can he no assessment on them. The assessment is a Charge in respect of income of the previous year. The individual assessees have ordinarily to. be living persons. The individual assessments are only for the purpose of computation of the income and are not a charge on the income of. the year of assessment. The individualess has to be assessed in the year of account in which the income is received. Ellie C. Re. B. M. Kamdar, , referred, to. The income which was sought to be assessed and which was held not to have been received in the year in which it was received was not liable under section 24 B(1) to be assessed. The High Court rightly answered the question in the negative and against the Commissioner of Income Tax. Ellies Brothers & Co Ltd. vs C.I.T., Bombay, , referred (ii) to. The respondents were not liable under the section to be taxed as income in respect of their income for the year in question.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. They challenged the Act and the Rules and the proposed action as ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioners contended that article 16(3) under which the Act and Rules purported to be made had been misunderstood as conferring a power to make a law prescribing requirement as to residence in a part of a State. The Act, the Rules and its proposed action were ultra vires the constitution. The respondents contended that article 15(1) of the Constitution had no application to the State of Andhra Pradesh and that the Act and its Rules were ultra vires. HELD : The contention must be rejected. Article 15(1), which was a special provision, was intended to give protection to the weaker sections of the people. The word 'State ' in article 12 was to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word in article 12. The second clause then specified a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. The third pause then made an exception. This clause was amended by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956. The clause was amended in the following terms: "Under any State specified in the First Schedule or any local or other authority within its territory any requirement as to the residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment shall be the same as is specified in the first schedule. " The clause was again amended by the Constitu tion (Seventh Amend ment) Act, 1955. The clause now made a declaration that no person shall be disqualified for any office in the territory of India because of his residence in any particular part of India. The exception, therefore, must be viewed narrowly and not carried to excess by interpretation. The article speaks of residence in a State and means only that. If it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as District, Talauqa, cities, towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used such as 'any requirement as to 'residence within that State ' or Union territory '. Having used the word State, the unit State is only meant and not any part thereof. [121 B D] The contention that the requirement may be also as to residence within the State or any particular part thereof was misconceived. The words 'any requirement ' cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. The fact that this clause is an exception and came as an amendment must dictate that a narrow construction upon the exception should be placed as indeed the debates in the Constituent Assembly also seem to indicate. [122 B C]

The appellant was charged with having committed an offence under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898. The prosecution case was that the appellant had secreted five registered letters in the house of the Sub Inspector of Post Office, and that the appellant was in possession of these letters. The appellant denied the charge and stated that he had no connection with the post office and that he had been falsely implicated. The Additional Sessions judge acquitted the appellant of the charge under section 52 but convicted him under section 52. The High Court held that the appellant 's possession of the letters was not proved and that the conviction was not justified. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The mere fact of possession does not suffice to show that the letters were secreted by the appellant. The mere fact that the letters contained certain other articles belonging to the appellant could not justify the conclusion that he had secreted them from the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which was said to have been in the appellant ' 's exclusive possession. [413 B C] (ii) The object of the provision is to prevent postal articles 'in course of transmission by post ' from being tampered with and so the secreting, destruction etc., of postal articles to which the provision is directed is to such secreting, ' destruction etc., as would frustrate or tend to frustrate their delivery to the addressees. [417 B C] In the present case, the appellant had been in possession of the articles for an inordinate length of time and the mere fact of his possession was not sufficient to show that he had committed any of the acts specified in section 52. [418 B C] The appellant could not be said to have secreted the letters just because it was found in the Almirah which is said to have behaved in his exclusive possession. The mere possession of the article is not sufficient to prove that the article was in his exclusive ' possession. [419 B C] 414 (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could have been convicted under section 52 without the Court having to consider whether he had secreed the articles. [419 D] (iv) The appellant had been convicted under the provisions of section 52 of Act. The appellant could have no grievance that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of the provisions of sections 103 and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [420 B] (v) The High 'Court was right in convicting the appellant under section 52 and the sentences passed against him were not excessive. [420 C] (vi) The appellant could be convicted under section 53 of the Act. [420 D] (vii) The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in section 342 of the Code. [420 E] (viii) The High court was right in acquitting the appellant of all the charges. [420 F]

The Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas, District Deoria, passed an order staying proceedings before it. The Nyaya Panchayat was not satisfied for want of evidence by way of proper affidavit etc. The N affirmation was accepted by the High Court. The Natidars, who were present in Court, made an application to the Court and signed it before it. It was alleged that the Nyaya Panchayat had proceeded with the case. The Nanchait Panchas, who were also present, made an applica tion to the Court that the N affirmation be taken on record. The Court passed an order that the Natidhar Panchayat should proceed with the case and that the Nanchaits should not proceed with the proceedings. The Nakshatn Panchas did not accept the application and the Court passed an adverse order against the Nyaya Panchayats. The Naksha Panchas, however, did not accept it and the Nyaya Panchas filed an application before the Nyaya panchayat for staying proceedings. The High Court admitted the application and stayed proceedings. The Panchas did nothing of the kind. The Nabhast Panchas, in their affidavits, stated that the Nakshatna Panchas had to authority to tell the Panchas that their affidavit was not proper. The High court held that the Nabhast Panchayats exercised judicial powers and even if the Panchas erred in not staying proceedings before the N affirmation, before finding them guilty of contempt of court, it should be presumed that the Naksha Panchaars had knowledge of the order of the High Court and that the Panchas had knowledge of it. The High. Court, however, held that the Panchaars did not believe the contents of the application and affidavit and that the matter should be decided on the basis of the evidence. The High, Court disbelieved the explanation of the Panchas and held that the order of stay was not passed deliberately to circumvent the order of High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court did not appreciate that the Nlok Panchas were not well versed in law and procedure and the records maintained by them should not be judged in the same manner as that of ordinary courts. The High Courts are not bound to do so and if they bona fide did not in their discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that they have committed contempt of court. [120 G] (ii) The High Courts should not have drawn an adverse inference from the fact that the reasons for not accepting the prayer for stay were not recorded. [121 B] (iii) The High court should not have drew an adverse inference against the Panchas because the reasons for their non acceptance were not recorded and the Panchas did. not appear to have been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. [121 C] (iv) The High.Court did not appreciate the facts and the High Court had not kept in mind the principles which should be kept in mind in dealing with the evidence. [121 D]

The appellant was charged with the murder of one Sheo Sahai. The prosecution case was that the appellant had a motive to harm Sheo Sahai and that he had purchased a sword and had deposited it at the Police Station. The appellant denied the allegation that he had caused the death of Sheo Sahai and alleged that he was falsely accused of the offence. The Sessions Judge believed the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and convicted the appellant. The High Court did not rely on the extra judicial confession of the appellant and did not rely upon the extra judicial confessions of the appellant. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report to the Police. The High court did not rely of the extra judicial confessional statement of the appellant but relied on certain portions of the report which did not amount to a direct admission of the appellant 's striking Sheo Sahai with a sword and thereby causing his death. The High, Court did not consider the evidence of any of the prosecution witness as to the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword by the appellant. Held, that the High Court erred in rejecting the statement of the accused 's confession. The extra judicial confession is not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. The murder was committed in the month of June. Both on account of the temperature and on account of a culprit 's desire to wash of blood marks on his person, the appellant ' 's bathing in the Canal at that hour of the night cannot be said to be improbable. It is not stated by the sub Inspector of Police or the appellant that the appellant bad on his person or on his clothes blood stains when he presented himself at the Police station. The fact that he had the sword which was stained with human blood, leads to such a supposition, even if the mere possession of a sword so stained be not sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder. The Canal runs beside the field. Ujagar Singh was on the field for the purpose of watching it against the neel gais trespassing and grazing the crop. It is therefore not a matter of surprise that he wakes up and proceeds to the spot from where the splashing sound which is supposed to be due to the wading of the neel glabis came. On reaching the Canal bank, he observes the person bathing and naturally asks him what led him to have a bath at that hour at night. Taken by surprise, it is not unlikely that the appellant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the Police Station and report the matter there. It is true that the appellant did not rush to the village at once and convey the news of the murder of Sheo Sahai. It is also unusual that a person who commits a murder in pursuance of an enmity arising out of minor disputes would be feeling so justified in his conduct as to openly admit it to the first person he met and to go to the Police station and report about it. It is always difficult to find reasons for a person 's acting in a certain manner. It may be that having blurted out the truth to Ujagar Singh, when taken by surprise, the appellant thought that the best thing he could have done was to proceed to Police Station and reported the matter there, and that he did so in circumstances which might lead to a reasonable belief that he had committed the offence. Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant ' s confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai has been erroneously rejected by the High Court.

The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the election of the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December, 1978 under the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya pradesh Municipal Corporation Rules, 1963 was not in accordance with the provisions of Rule 4(3) of the Rules and that the election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice. The High court also held that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution on account of inordinate delay in the presentation of the writ petition. The High Courts order was challenged by the appellants in this Court. The appellants contended that the notice under Rule 4 (1) of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporations (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963 notifying that claims and objections should be preferred within a period of 20 days from the date of the publication of the notice, was issued on September 30, 1978 and that the writ petition was filed on December 28, 1978. The respondents contended that the writ petitions were not maintainable as the period of limitation prescribed for filing the writ petition had expired on December 30, 1978. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High courts have the power to issue an appropriate writ under Article 226, and the power of the High Court under Article 226 to issue an order under Article 226 is discretionary and if the High Court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of the writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. [495G H] 2. The power of the Court under Article 227 of the Constitution to issue an injunction is discretionary and the High Court is not bound to exercise its discretion in every case. The High, Court is not justified in refusing to exercise its jurisdiction under Article 226 merely because the petitioner has an alternative remedy. [496B] 3. The power under Article 226 has to be exercised judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [497B] 4. The power is discretionary and it is not necessary that the High Court should exercise the same in every case or every case. [499B] 5. The power to issue a writ under Article 227 is discretionary and is not to be exercised in a routine manner. The High. Court is not to act as a court of appeal under Article 226 and the only way in which it can exercise its discretion is to refuse to exercise its power. [494C] 6. The power conferred on the High Court by Article 226 is a discretionary power. The High 'Court is not to exercise its powers in a routine way. It is not to refuse to consider the justness of the claim of the petitioner merely because it is lawful to do so. The High COurt is not to re examine the matter as an appellate court. [498B C] 7. The High High Court is entitled to refuse to issue an interim order if it finds the petition to be frivolous or vexatious or that the petitioner is guilty of overawing the court. [498A] 8. The High Cour 's power under Article 227 has to be exercise judiciously and reasonable in the circumstances of the case. [498B] 9. The power in the High Courts under Article 226 cannot be used to upset the well established principles of law or to supplant the settled position. [498C] 10. The power has to be used sparingly and only in appropriate cases. [498D] 11. The High] Court is not entitled to refuse relief to the petitioner on the ground that he has an alternative or additional remedy. [498E] 12. The High; Court is not expected to act under Article 226 as a court ' of appeal. The High .Court is not expected in the exercise of its jurisdiction under article 226 to act as an appellate Court. [498F] 13. The High: Court is not a court of general jurisdiction in the matter of issuing writs. The High ]/ Court is not called upon to exercise its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 136. [498G] 14. The High The Court is not exercising its jurisdiction under Art 226 of the Constitu tion. The High the Court is not sitting as a court or as a court. The High ,Court is not exercising the powers of an appellate court under Article 226. The High is not exercising an appellate jurisdiction. The High cannot, therefore, be called upon to act under article 226. [498H; 499A] 15. The High shall not, however, exercise this power if the petitioner has already moved the High Court in that behalf. [405B] 16. The High may not be justified in refusing relief to the petitioners on the ground of laches in the writ petition, but the High Court has to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction in the facts and circumstances of the present case. [500B]

The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1953. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which was punishable under sub section (3) of that section, were laid before a general meeting of the company. The balance sheets and profit and lost accounts of the company were laid before the company at the general meeting. The company was not in a position to send the balance sheet and the profit and loss accounts to the Registrar of Companies. The company had a large staff of directors and the directors were not in a financial position to send their balance sheets and profits and loss accounts. The company did not send the balance sheets and the profit & loss account to the Registrar. The company filed a complaint against the respondent company and its directors for failure to comply with the provisions of section 220(4) of the . The trial court convicted the respondent company under section 134(4) and section 220(3) of the Act. The High Court, in appeal, held that the company and its Directors could not rely on their failure to send the general body meeting as a defence to the prosecution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the company was not liable under section 134 (4) of that Act. The company and its director could not rely upon their failure to call the general body meetings as a defence. Under section 134(2) of the 1913 Act, the laying of the balance sheet before the company in the general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents should be filed before the Registrar. If no general body meeting was held, the persons concerned could not be said to have committed a default in complying with those provisions. [414 B C] The provisions of section 134(1) (2) of that statute are clear and unambiguous. The requirement of section 134 (2) is that the balance sheet should be laid before the general meeting of a company. The requirement is that the company should send a copy of the balance sheets to the Registrar, and the failure to do so is made punishable under section 134. [414 D E] The difference in language is very clear and pointed. The responsibility of sending three copies of the balance of the profit and lost account arises only after they have been laid before the Company at the general meet ing. Without laying the balance sheet, the persons are not in a 'position to send their accounts to the registrar. The failure to send a copy is made punishable by section 134(3). [415 B C] In the instant case, the company did not sent the balance sheet to the Registrar and the profit& and loss account were not laid before the Registrar, but were sent to the Registrar after the company had been placed under the control of the Registrar. [415 D] The State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. ; , referred to. The provisions of sections 32 and 133 of the 1913 and section 134 of the 1913 are clear and explicit. The responsibility to send three copies of balance sheet and profits and lost accounts arises only after the balance sheet has been laid before a company at the annual general meeting. [415 E] The provisions in section 134(5) of the 1956 Act are clear and clear. The requirement that the balance of profit and loss should be sent to the regis tered shareholders only after they had been laid before it is a condition for the application of section 134. The failure of the company to send the profit and losses account to the registrars after they had already been laid before them is a condition under section 134 and the company is not liable under that section. [415 F]

The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, was enacted to provide for the speedier trial of certain offences. The Act provided for the establishment of a special court for the trial of offences specified in the Schedule to the Act. The Act was amended by the West Bengal Special Court (Amendment) Act, 1952, which by section 5(1) provided that the Special Court shall try such offences or classes of offences or cases or classes of cases as the State Government may, by general or special order in writing direct. The Act also provided for the appointment of a special judge to preside over the trial of cases. The Act, however, did not provide for the appointment or appointment of a judge to a Special Court. The Act empowered the State Government to direct "cases" to be tried by a Special Court and the State Government could direct "call for cases" and "call" for "case" and "case" together. The Act did not provide that the Special Judge could try "cases", "classes of offences" or "classes or classes of cages" or "cases". The Act also did not provide any machinery for the appointment and transfer of the Special Judge. The Act gave the Special Judge the power to try "call cases" and to transfer cases to him. The Act thus conferred on the Special Judge a discretion to choose which cases he should try and the discretion was not absolute but was subject to judicial review. The Act in so far as it empowered the State Govern ment to direct "Cases" to he tried by a special court, was void. The Act could not be challenged on the ground of violation of article 14 of the Constitution. The Act had no application to the present case as the classification of offences was not based on any intelligible differentia and had no relation to the object of the Act. It was not a case of classification of offences based on any differentia and the Act did not violate article 14 of ' the Constitution. The workmen of the appellant company were paid a minimum wage of Rs. 84 per month. The company was paying a minimum wage at Rs. 95 per month. In the year 1962 63 the company was paying Rs. 95 as minimum wage. In the next year the company was paid Rs. 95. The workmen claimed that the company should be paid Rs. 94 as minimum wage and that the company be directed to pay Rs. 94. The company resisted the claim on the ground that the company was not a 'State ' within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution and that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to fix the minimum wage. The Tribunal held that the company would be entitled to Rs. 95 only as minimum wage, and that the minimum wage should be fixed at Rs. 94 per month. On appeal by the workmen the company contended that the Tribunal committed an error in fixing the minimum wage at the rate of Rs. 95 and that the workmen should be paid the minimum wage of the minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the company could not be allowed to raise the dispute regarding the minimum wage for the first time in the year 1962. The principle of fixation of wages on the basis of the living wage being the highest in the region where the industry was producing the same kind of work, the Tribunal was justified in fixing the wage in the region. The concept of minimum wage, does take in the factor of the prevailing cost of essential commodities whenever such minimum wage is to be fixed. It may be noticed that by the very nature of employment being casual, it can be presumed that a casual worker is on a lower footing and cannot expect the same wages as a permanent employee. Therefore, the decision of the Tribunal not to equate the casual workers with the permanent employees was correct. The Tribunal had directed that the increase of Rs. 12 p.m. in the total minimum wage packet allowed by it will enure to the benefit of the lowest paid female, badi and permanent dailyrated workers also. The company had agreed to exclude these classes of workers in regard to payment of bonus. The Tribunal was not justified in fixing Rs. 94 p.m., as the minimum wage, as the minimum wages were not fixed at the same level as the basic wage. The principle which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate three months ' basic wage in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account. The Tribunal rejected the demand for higher bonus on the ground of the application of the Full Bench Formula. The Tribunal did not commit any error of law in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties. The principle that is being applied in the present case is the simple principle of calculating the minimum wage payable at the minimum wage in the present region. The principle is that the minimum wages should be fixed on the basis Of the living wage and not on the basis as in the case of the living wages. The principle was not applicable to the present case as the company was a 'State " within the meaning Of article 12 of Constitution. The principle has no application to the present dispute. The principle cannot be applied to the present matter as the company had agreed specifically to exclude the workmen in regard to the payment of bonus and the Tribunal was not right in fixing the amount of minimum wage at a lesser level than the basic wage in the case. The principle, therefore, cannot be applied in the instant case. The Tribunal has not committed any error of jurisdiction in fixing the rate of minimum wage. [677 D] The Associated Cement Companies Ltd. vs Its Workmen, ; , referred to. The workmen were entitled to the minimum wage as fixed by the award. The Tribunal should have fixed the minimum wage on the basis that the workmen were entitled as of right to the same wages and should not have fixed the same wage in the absence of any agreement between the parties. The assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The Income tax Officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income tax Act, 1961, to the assessee, calling upon it to produce its books of account and other relevant papers. The assessee produced before the Income tax Officer a statement showing various creditors from whom it had borrowed on Hundi during the accounting year in question. The Income Tax Officer, after enquiry, found that the assessee had borrowed a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ from various parties of Calcutta and that the assessee 's transactions were bogus. He issued a notice to the assessee under section 148. The assessee challenged the validity of the notice as well as the proceedings taken on the strength of that notice on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The notice was issued after four years but before eight years of the date of the original assessment. Section 148 prescribes a period of four years from the end of the relevant assessment year, before which the Income tax officer should record his reasons for doing so. The notice was therefore issued after four year. [445 D] The notice was not issued in accordance with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. The Income ' tax Officer had not stated in the report that he had satisfied himself that the assessee was a fit case to issue the notice under section 147. The material that he had before him for issuing the notice under s. 148 is not mentioned in the report. In his report he vaguely refers to certain communications received by him from the C.I.T., Bihar and Orissa. He does not mention the facts contained in those communications. He has not even come to a prima facie conclusion that the transactions to which he referred are not genuine transactions. He has merely stated that he was satisfied that the transactions were bogus transactions. Such a conclusion does not fulfil the requirements of s. 151(2). What that provision requires is that he must give reasons for issuing a notice under s 148. In other words he must have some prima facie grounds before him for taking action under s.148. Further his report mentions that he was not satisfied that the assessee has escaped assessment for that year. [446 G H; 447 A B]

The appellant 's father, who was a member of a joint Hindu family, died in 1960 leaving behind him his widow and two daughters. The appellant 's mother died in 1960 and the appellant 's brother, the first respondent, was born in 1960. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties and for a declaration that the suit properties belonged to the joint family and were in the possession of the appellant and his brother. The appellant contended that the suit was not maintainable as the suit properties did not belong to the joint Hindu family and that the suit property did not belong exclusively to the joint Family. The trial court dismissed the suit. The first appellate court held that the suit lands belonged to the family and that there was no prior partition between the appellant and the other members of the family. The High Court in second appeal held that the appellant ' 's mother 's interest in the coparcenary property would devolve by intestate succession under the Act and not by survivorship and that the appellant was entitled to a 7/24th share. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit for partition was not maintainable because (i) the suit properties were not joint family properties but were the self acquisitions of the appellant ' and his brother and (ii) the suit property was not the joint family property but the joint family house. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Hindu Succession Act came into force on June 17, 1956. The appellant and his mother were governed by the Mitakshara School of Hindu Law. The appellant was entitled under the Hindu Succession Act to a share in the joint family pro perty. [767B] (2) The Hindu Law on the question of intestate succession is that the property of a male Hindu dying intestate devolves according to the provisions of the Act in the order specified in the Act. Section 6 of the Act provides that the property devolving on a Hindu female who has not completed the age of 18 years shall be held by her as a full owner. [767C] (3) The Hindu Women 's Rights to Property Act, 1937, which was enacted by the Hindu Succession, provides by section 14(1) that any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of the Act, shall be held as a full and absolute owner. [677C] (4) The Hindu women 's right to property is not a mere personal right but a property right. The right to property accrues to the husband by virtue of his having a wife and children. The right is personal to the husband and the property is his self acquired property. The right of the widow to maintenance is not a personal right but is a right to property. [674D] (5) The Hindu widow 's right is not a purely personal one. It is a right arising out of the property of the joint Hindu Family. It is property which is capable of being disposed of by a will or other testamentary disposition. The right which a Hindu widow has under the Hindu Law to maintenance is a personal obligation so far as the members of the joint Family are concerned and it is not a property in the hands of a person other than the husband. [676E] (6) The Hindu female 's right of maintenance is not confined to the mere right to recover the property in the manner provided in the Act but it is a tangible right against property which flows from the family as a complete owner. [678B] (7) The Hindu wife 's right under the Hindu Women ' 's Rights Act, 1937 to maintenance is personal to her and is not a chose in action. [678C] (8) The Hindu Widow 's Estate Act, 1905, which was passed by the Bombay Legislature in 1805, provides by cl. (1) that the widow 's estate shall, subject to the provisions contained in the Act, be capable of being transferred and encumbered for her life time. [679B] (9) The Hindu law on the question as to intestate succession has to be decided on the basis of the provisions of section 6 of the Hindu Succession. [679C] (10) The Hindu succession Act, 1956, which came into force in 1956, provides by s. 14(1)(a) that the property in Hindu Mitakshara coparcenery shall be held in the order of succession specified in the Schedule. [679D] (11) The Hindu Mitaksharta School of Hindu law, which is a recognised and accepted school of Hindu law and which has been recognised by the Hindu Law Commission in its report of 1955, has adopted a rule of Hindu law that the property inherited by a female from her father or other male relative, which is not the case here, is to be treated as property belonging to her husband and as such to be possessed by her as such and by virtue of section 6(1) of the Hindu succession Act the property is to be held in that order of succession. [679E] (12) The Hindu Married Women 's Right to Property Act. 1937, which is enacted by the Bombay legislature in 1937, provides by sub section (1) of section 14 that the widow shall be entitled to live in the property of her husband during his life time and after his death to the possession and enjoyment of all his movable and immovable property. [679F] (13) The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 which was enacted in 1956 provides by section 18 that the widow of a Hindu male shall be entitled, subject to certain restrictions, to maintenance out of any property which she has acquired before her death and section 18A(1) provides that any property acquired by a Hindu female after the date of commencement of the 1956 Act shall be held on her own behalf by her husband and not by her as an heir. [680B] (14) The Hindu Act applies to the property of an intestate Hindu male who dies after the commencement. of the Act. [681C] (15) The Hindu woman 's right in the joint Hindu Mitaksra coparcener 's property is not confined only to the right to recover property in the nature of a right of maintenance. It is also a tangible right in favour of the husband and against the wife. [689D] (16) The Hindu Hindu Women ' Rights to Property and Maintenance Act. 1956, which was a pre existing Act, provides by sections 3 and 4 that the property possessed by the Hindu female shall be held for the benefit of the husband, and the widow, and that the widow is entitled to hold the property for her own benefit.
