The respondent, an employee of the appellant Corporation, was promoted to Class I post in 1963. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Manager in 1965. He was further promoted to the next higher post of Manager in 1969. In the year 1965, the Corporation framed the (Staff) Regulations, 1965, which were applicable to the employees of the Corporation. Regulation 19(2) provided that the age of retirement of the employees of a Corporation shall be 60 years. The respondent was promoted to class I post in the year 1963. In the writ petition filed by him, the High Court held that the respondent was entitled to continue in service till he attained the age of 60 years as other Class I employees belonging to the category of transferred employees. The Corporation appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent was entitled under Regulation 19(1) of the (Stage I) Regulations, 1960 to continue in the service till he completed the age of 58 years. [223B] 1.2 The respondent was not entitled to continue to be in service beyond the age of superannuation in the year 1965. [223C] 1.3 The respondent was governed by the terms and conditions of service applicable to him at the time of his promotion to Class I. The terms and conditions were not in any way different from those applicable to the other employees of the Corpo ration. The respondent had been promoted to Class II post in 1963 and was governed by Regulation 19(3) of the Regulations, which provided that the conditions of service of an employee of a Corpo ration shall be such as may be prescribed by the Regulations. The Regulations were framed under the Act. Regulation 19 of the Regulations was amended in 1977, and Regulation 19(4) was added to the Regulations. Regulation 19 was given retrospective effect from 20th June, 1979. The fact that the pay, allowances and other conditions of service had been made the same in respect of both the transferred employees and the employees of Corpora tion recruited after 1st September, 1956 has not brought about the integration of the two classes of employees into one cadre. Even the High Court in the instant case accepted that it was just and proper to extend the benefit of the higher age of retirement to the trans ferred employees but it has held that when once a trans ferred employee was promoted to a Class I post, he would lose the right to a special treatment as regards the age of superannua tion. [223D G] 2.1 The High Court erred in striking down regulation 19(2). The respondent was bound to retire at the age of 55 years. The High Court was not justified in holding that when once the trans fer was promoted, he would be entitled to continue till he attained 60 years. [224B] 2.2 The High Court has not considered the question whether the age of retire ment of employees who have joined the service of the Corpora tional would be raised to 60 years. That is a matter of policy which has got to be decided by the Corporation and the Central Government. [224C] 3.1 The decision taken by the Corporation as regards the ages of retirement of its employees is a bona fide one and cannot be characterised as unreasonable. It is not, therefore, liable to be upset by a decision of the Court. [224D] 3.2 The decision taken in the instant cases is a bona fid one and cannot, therefore, be characterised as arbitrary. [224E] 3.3 The High Court, in the instant ease, erred in striking the said regulation 19(1). [224F] 4.1 The Corporation is a public sector undertaking. The employees of the respondent were governed by the provisions of the Act. The Corporation framed the Staff Regulations, 1965 and the Regulations were framed in exercise of the powers conferred by section 48(2) of the Act, which were in force at the relevant time. Regulation 19 provides that the age for retirement of an employee shall be 60. Regulation 19 is given retrospective effect. The fact of the respondent having been promoted to the Class I post of Assistant Manage ment in 1963 and having been governed by Regulation 18(1) would not make any difference. The petitioner, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1953 54. The Income tax Officer, in the course of the assessment proceedings, found that the petitioner had evaded payment of income tax on the income of the company and that the petitioner was, therefore, liable to be proceeded against under section 34 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the Act was discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution, (2) that the procedure prescribed by the Act in regard to persons similarly situate with those who are proceeded with under section 34 is substantially different from the procedure prescribed under the Indian Income Tax Act, and (3) that the provisions of the Act in so far as they affect the persons proceeded against under the Act are discriminatory and void. Held, that the procedure laid down in the Act in sections 6 and 7 is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure prescribed in the Indian Incometax Act and, therefore, the Act offends against the provisions of article 14. The procedure prescribed by section 5(4) of the Act is substantially prejudicial, to the assessee. The procedure laid down by the Act is not substantially prejudicial to a person who is dealt with under section 5(1) of the Indian Incometax Act and whose income is sought to be assessed under section 34. The procedure under section 5 (4) is not substantially different from that under section 34 and the procedure prescribed is substantially prejudicial. The procedure in section 5(5) is not discriminatory and does not offend article 14 of Constitution. The procedure, therefore, is not discriminatory. The procedure is not discriminatory if it is not substantially more drastic than the procedure under section 34, and the procedure in section 34 is not discriminatory when it is substantially more drastic. The procedure provided by the Act does not contravene article 14 of. The procedure for reference under section 5 is not substantially less drastic than the one under section 34 but is more drastic than that under section 5. The procedure thus prescribed in section 5 (5) is substantially prejudicial and is not discriminatory, and is not therefore discriminatory. The provisions of section 5(2) and section 5(3) of the impugned Act are not discriminatory and do not offend article. 14 of the constitution. The procedure of the Commission under section 5 of the Act does, not contravene article 20(3) Of the Constitution. The provisions in section 5 of Act are not violative of article 20(1) Of the constitution. Section 5(4), which is a special provision, is not violative of the provisions of that article. The procedure to be followed by the Commission is provided in section 5 and section 5 (1) of Act. The procedure so prescribed is not discriminatory as the procedure prescribed for assessment under section 34 does not contravene the provisions of section 34. Section 5 (4), which provides that the procedure under the section shall be followed in respect of the same person, is not therefore violative of article, 20(3). The procedure prescribed in section 34 of Act is substantially different in its nature and character from that prescribed under section 5, and the provisions of sections 5(2), 5(3), 5(4). and 5(5), are not discriminatory. Section 5 of the impugned section is not discriminatory in that it does not provide for the procedure to be adopted in respect of persons who are dealt with under the section. The procedure specified in section 5 is a special procedure and is not violative article 14 of ' the Constitution. Section 5 is not discriminatory because it does not give any indication as to the procedure to he followed in the case of persons who have escaped assessment. The procedure established by the Act for the assessment of income of a person is not discriminatory unless it is found that the procedure is substantially more advantageous to the assessee and is more drastic and prejudicial to him. The procedure adopted in the present case is not discriminatory but is more prejudicial to the petitioner. The procedure followed in the present Case is not discriminatory since it does not contravene section 5(6) of the Income tax Act. The provisions contained in section 5 are not discriminatory because they do not give any guidance to the Commission in the matter of the procedure to, be followed in the assessment of the assessee. Section 5 does not contravene articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. There is no discrimination in the procedure prescribed. The procedure as prescribed in section 6 and 7 of the Act was substantially prejudicial to, the petitioner and was not discriminatory.

The respondent was a registered office under the Delhi and Ajmer Mercantile Co operative Bank Ltd. The activities carried on by the respondent No, 1 are a "trade or business" within the, meaning of section. 2(5). [353 C E] (3) The activity of the respondent is not a "business or trade" because by the Memorandum of Association, the respondent was not carrying on any business or trade in the premises in question. The activities undertaken by the respondent are not a "calling" or "service" of any kind. The activities do not bring the respondent 's premises within the definition. [353 F G] (4) The pre Premises of the appellant, is a " Commercial establishment" within. the meaning of the Act. [354 A] (5) The pre premise of the appellant 's business is a "trade" or "business" activity. The activities, therefore, of the respondent are a "commercial" establishment within the meaning. of section 2. (5) and section 2(19) of the . [354 B C] (6) The pre 'premises of the appellant has a "trade". The pre premises are a "call" or " service" of any type. The activities conducted by the respondent in the present appeal are a "business" or "trade" activity. [354 C D]

The respondent was the holder of a Jagir in the United Provinces. In 1796 there were certain disputes between him and the Zamindar of the district. The matter was referred to the Board of Revenue. The quantum of the pension was calculated on the basis of 1/4th of the revenue of the Jagir. The pension was paid regularly from year to year by the Government to the respondent. During the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50 the respondent received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ on account of the aforesaid pension. The Income tax Officer, in spite of the objection of the respondent, held that it was a regular annual income of the respondent and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and although the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appeared in the second degree, its immediate and effective source was the Government 's statutory obligation to pay it and this obligation was not land within the meaning of Income tax Act. He accordingly held that the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determined with respect to the quantum of the rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. " The respondent appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the alleged cash grant of varying and unspecified amount received by the respondent in relation to land revenue of Seyedpur now Tehsil of District Ghazipur, clearly fell within the definition of agricultural income under section 2(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The respondent appealed, to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal which held that the amount received by him was a regular income of the assessee and did not fail within the category Of agricultural income tax and that the income could not be held to be agricultural income for the purpose of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. The High Court, on a reference, held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837, it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. It relied on the fact that the amount which had been received by the successors of the respondent varied from year to years. The High court accordingly answered the question in the negative. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The income in question was not agricultural Income as defined in the Act. (ii) The source of the allowance or pension was the arrangement arrived at in 1837. The income could not therefore be held to have been derived from land within the definition in section 2(i)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act and the income could be held to fall within the definition. (iii) The allowance was revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. The appellant will have his costs here and in the High Court. Per Hidayatullah, J. (i) In the present case the source of the right in which a fraction of the net income of the trust was to be appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration was not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands, but rest of the income from the trust property. The income of the Trust appropriated by the assessee as remuneration was not received by him as rent or revenue or agricultural income. (ii). The allowance was in fact a payment of the compensation for relinquishing the title to those lands. The allowance was not taxable income as agricultural income and was not exempt from tax.

The appellants in the Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors 'A ' in the Indian Ordnance Factories on different dates between the years 1962 and 1963. The appellants in the writ petition filed in the Madhya Pradesh High Court were appointed as Chargeman II in the year 1964. The appellants were promoted as Chargeman II on the basis of the seniority cum merit. The respondents in the writ petitions filed in the High Court were the Union of India through the Director General of Ordnance Factories. The appellants of Civil Appeal No 441 of 1981 claimed that they were entitled to be promoted to the post of Chargeman II on completion of 2 years of service as Supervisor 'A ' and that they were not given the benefit of automatic promotion in violation of the constitutional guarantee under Article 16 of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and directed the Union of india to promote the appellants to the post. The Union of India appealed to this Court by way of special leave. The appellants contended that the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of the order dated 2nd February, 1981 as they had not been granted the benefit of promotion in violation thereof. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The order dated 28th December, 1965 which provided a minimum period of service of three years in the lower grade for promotion to the next higher grade and the circular dated 20th January, 1966 which provided that promotions in future would be made in accordance with the normal rules and not merely on compl ete basis on completion of two years ' satisfactory service had the effect of doing away with the accelerated chance of promotion and rele vant ly, the right to promotion on the basis thereof was to be governed by the Rules. The order of the High Court dated 2nd Febru ary, 1981 was, therefore, not in accordance with law. [103D E] 1.2 The order dated 2 nd February, 1981 was not in conflict with the order dated 28 th December, 1965. The order had been superseded by the later order dated 20th Januar y, 1966. The order was, therefore not in conflict wit h the order dated 20 th January, 1966. [103F G] 1.3 The order dated 20.1.1981 was not in accord ance with law. The order did not confer any legal right on the appellants. The appellants had been given a back date promotion to the post in question. The appellants, therefore, had no right to be promoted on the basis that they had been promoted on the date on which they ought to have been promoted. [103G H] 1.4 The appellants were entitled to the same relief as was granted to the other similarly situated persons in the writ peti tions before the Madhya Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh High Courts. [104A] 1.5 The appellants in Civil Appeal No, 441 of 1981 had been promoted as Chargeman I in the year 1963 and 1964 respectively. The appellants have been given a further promotion to the said post in the year 1966. The appellants are, therefore, entitled to the said promotion with effect from the date on whi ch they ought to be promoted. [104B C] 1.6 The appellants in C.A. No. 441/81 have been given back date promotion on the ground that they have not been granted their back wages and promotion to higher posts on the basis o f their back date promotion as Chargeman I. The appellants would, therefore, be entitled to the difference of back wages and salary from the date of promotion to the date of actual promotion. [104D E] 2. The appellants will be entitled to all consequential benefits. [104F] 3. The appellants shall also be entitled to costs. [104G] Civil Appeal No: 441 of 1981 is allowed in part. The respondents are directed to give the appellants the same relief which was granted to them in the writ petitioners before the Madhya Prade sh High Court. [104H; 105A] Civil Appeal Nos. 441 of 81 are dismissed. [105B] 3.1 The appellants in both the appeals are entitled to the relief granted by the High Court. The appellants may also be granted the same relief. [105C] 3.2 The appellants in civil appeal No. 441 are also entitled to the pay and allowances as per the rules. [105D] 3.3 The appellants in all the appeals are also entitled for the same relief granted to the others. [105E] 3.4 The respondents are further directed to give to the appellants the difference of salary and allowances from the date they ought to he promoted to the date on the basis on which they were actually promoted.
