The Karnataka State Transport Authority granted two permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, one to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation and two permits to Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation. The Karnataka State Transport Corporation filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the grant of two permits to it. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. The Karnataka Government issued a notification under section 63(7) of the authorising the Karnataka State Transport Development Corporation to operate on the route in question. The Karnataka Transport Corporation filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the grant to it of two permits. The High court allowed the writ petition and quashed the grant of the two permits to Corporation. The High Courts order was confirmed by this Court. The Karnataka Road Transport Corporation filed an appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High courts order is set aside and the Karnataka State Road transport Corporation is directed to reconsider the applications of the Corporation for two permits in accordance with law. [1016C] 2. The Karnataka Legislature enacted the Karnataka State Legislature 's Transport Act, 1957, which was enacted to provide for the development of road transport in the State of Karnataka. Section 47(1) of the Act provides that a permit granted by the Regional Transport Authority of any one region shall not be valid in any other region unless the permit has been counter signed by the Regional. Transport Authority of that other region, and a permit granted in any one State shall not be validity in any other State unless countersigned by the State Transport Authority of the other State or by the Regional 'Transport Authority concerned. Section 47 (1) (c) provides that the State Government may, by notification, constitute a State Transport Authority and appoint a Secretary to the State Transport authority. Section 47 is a provision with whose interpretation and vires the Act is primarily concerned in this case. [1017C E] 3. The proviso to section 47(1), for example, provides that other conditions being equal, an application for a stage carriage permit from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given preference over applications from individual owners. There is no problem here since the proviso itself says that the rules of preference will apply only if other conditions are equal. [1018B C] 4. The proviso is a rule of preference and not a rule of exclusion. When the Undertaking applies for permit under Chapter IV, it must satisfy the Regional Transport Autho rity that it is better suited than the private operator to render transport facility to the travelling public. [1019D] 5. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka State road transport Corporation and the private operators who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government, because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to section 63(1) the proper course for the Tribunal and the Court was to consider the claims of eligible applicants in the manner indicated in Sher Singh 's case. [1015E] 6. The State Government has not questioned the grant of any certificate of approval to the Central Government. The State Road Transport Authority has to consider the applications for stage carriage permits under section 47(2) of the and the private operator has an equal chance to get a permit even on inter State route if it shows that the Undertaking is either unable to provide efficient and economical service or that the private operator is better equipped to render the same. Preference in this context would mean that other things generally appearing to be qualitatively and quantitatively equal though not with mathematical accuracy, statutory provision will tilt the balance in favour of the Undertaking. [1020B C] 7. The High, Courts have failed to notice that the State Transport Appellate Tribu nal and the High Courts have failed in their duty to give reasons for their decisions. [1021B] 8. The High. Courts have failed even to notice that there is no guidelines as to how the discretion to grant approval is to be exercised once the minimum conditions are fulfilled. The matter appears to be left to the total discretion of the Central Government virtually as we said, pre empting the decision of the statutory tribunal. [1022B] 9. The clause pre empts the decision of a designated tribunal by executive discretion. It was said that the clause contained sufficient guidelines for the exercise of discretion in granting approval by the Central Government and the object of the proviso to section 1018 63(7). [1022C] 10. The High ' Courts order is set. aside and the State Transport Authority is directed to consider the application of the Corporation in accordance with the law. [1123B]

The respondent purchased by a registered instrument the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name and style of All India Trading Company. The respondent denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The respondent appealed to the Commercial Tax Officer as well as to the Board of Revenue but the appeals were dismissed. The respondent then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ in the nature of certiorari quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Reve nue. The High Court held that Rule 21 A of the Sales Tax Rules was illegal and ultra vires and the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title Purushottam. The State Government appealed to this Court. HELD : Rule 21 A is beyond the rule making power of the State Government either under section 19(1) or section 19(2)(c) of the Act. It was not open to the State Government to rely on the instrument inter vivos between the transferor and the transferee and to contend that there was any contractual obligation between the transferee and the State Government who is not a party to the instrument. [665 B C] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T. ; , Chatturam vs C.l.T. Bihar, ; , followed. Badridas 'Daga vs C I.T. , , distinguished. The State of Madras vs K. G. section Balaswami Chettiar, , referred to. The word 'assessment ' in the scheme of sales tax and income tax legislation is a term of varying import. The word is used sometimes to mean the computation of income, sometimes the determination of the amount of tax payable, and sometimes the whole procedure laid down in the Income tax Act for imposing liability on the tax payer. As the judicial Committee observed in Badridas vs Commissioner of Income tax, , the words 'assess ' and 'assessment ' refer primarily to the computation of the amount. of income. In the context and background of other sections of the Act, the word 'assessment" used in section 19(3) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 21A is beyond the rules making power of State Government either section 19(l) or section 10(1) of the Sales tax Act. [667 B C]

The appellant was a jailor in the State of Bombay. He was served with a charge sheet for mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The enquiry officer found him guilty of the charge and the Inspector General of Prisons, after giving him a hearing, passed an order dismissing him from service. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened the provisions of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court in appeal held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of the enquiry report amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311(1) of the constitution. It also held that the appellant had not asked for a copy of that report and had not been prejudiced by the non supply of the report. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the failure to provide the copy of the report of the enquiry officer amounted to denial to reasonable opportunity contemplated under article 311(i) of the . [922 D] The State of Bombay vs H. C. Goel, ; , referred to. The State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 369, distinguished. Union of India vs H.C. Goel, [1964] 4 S.C R. 718, referred to. 922 The appellant was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State of Maharashtra and the State of Gujarat. As is well known, the State of Bom bay was reorganised into the above two States and the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 contained various provisions for the apportionment of assets and liabilities between the two States. The Bombay Reorganisation Act was enacted to give effect to the proposals of the States Reorganisation Commission. The Bombay Reorganisa tion Act, 1960, contained various provisions relating to the apportionment of the assets and liabilities of the States. The liability to pay arrears of pay was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than a breach of contract. [922 E G] The State was not liable to pay arrears to the appellant because the liability to pay salary was not a debt in respect of a contract. [925 B] The State had not suffered any loss because the appellant had been dismissed from service. [925 C] The State could not be said to have suffered any loss if the appellant was not given a copy of his report. The appellant was entitled to a decree for arrears of salary. [925 D]

The respondents were lessees of a coal mine in the State of Bihar. The appellant was the successor in interest of the original lessee. The respondents filed a suit for a declaration that the appellant had encroached upon their coal land and removed coal therefrom and prayed for a declaration of their title to the land. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the High Court decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The suit was barred by limitation. The respondents had knowledge of the appellant 's encroachment of their coal mines only in the year 1941 which was within three years of the date of the filing of the suit. The High Court was in error in holding that the suit was barred. [499 B C] The burden of proof in the former sense was on the respondents. A division beach of the Patna High Court in Sundarji Shivji vs Secretary of State for India, (1932) L.R. 59 I.A. 13, held that when a defendant in an action based on tort seeks to show that the suit is not maintainable by reason of the expiry of the statutory period of limitation, it is upon him to prove the necessary facts. But the burden is not on the defendant to prove the date when he came to know of the trespass. The burden is on the defendant in the former case to prove that he had knowledge of it within three years from the date of his coming to know of it. But in the latter case, the burden is on him to prove that the trespasser had knowledge of his title within three years. [500 B D] In the present case, the respondents had knowledge that the appellant was in possession of the coal mines only within three years prior to the filing of their suit. The appellant had not produced any evidence to show that he had any knowledge of the trespass within three years before the suit. [501 B C] Sundarji Shivjji vs Secretary Of State for India in Council, L.R., and Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, I.L.R. , referred to. The High Courts in India have consistently taken the view that the burden of proof lies on the person who asserts that a particular state of affairs exists and that the burden has been so laid on him that the onus is on him. [503 B C] In the instant case, the appellant had not discharged the burden. The High court was in error when it held that the burden was wrongly thrown on the appellant. [504 C] The High Court accepted the finding of the courts below that the respondents had no knowledge of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of the encroached land beyond three years prior thereto. But it did not hold that the respondents were entitled to claim exemption from the operation of rule 76 of the Indian Coal Mines Regulation, 1946, because, the respondents could not claim exemption from section 3 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, because, section 3 of that Act made it obligatory on a court to dismiss a suit barred by limitation, although limitation had not been set up as a defence, indicating thereby that it was the duty of a plaintiff to establish, at any rate prima facie, that the suit, was within time. [505 D E] The burden was on the appellant to prove that they had knowledge of their encroachment of their land and removal of coal therefrom within three years, within three years preceding the date of their suit, and the respondents had failed to discharge that burden. [506 B] The High Courts have consistently taken this view. [507 B]

The appellant was a workman in the State of Kerala. He was dismissed from service by the management on June 24, 1958, on the charge of misconduct. The appellant filed a dispute before the Industrial Tribunal, Kerala, which was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The Tribunal also held that the action taken under r 18(a), was a colourable exercise of the power given under that rule and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the powers under that rule. The appellant contended that it was entitled under r.18(a) to dispense with the service of any employee after complying with its terms. The Tribunal found that the appellant was not entitled under r 18 (a) to discharge him and set aside the order of discharge. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the appellant could not be allowed to raise the question of the validity of the discharge of his service under r. (a) of r. 18 of the Standing orders. The discharge of the appellant was bona fide and was not colourable. The appellant was not justified in raising the question of validity of the order of dismissal. The discharge was not mala fide. The Industrial Tribunal had the right to inquire into the causes that led to the termination of service under r 18. The Industrial Court had the right under r. 10(2) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Rules, 1950, to enquire into the causes which led to the discharge of the workman. The Industrial Courts had the right, under r. 12(2) to enquire into any alleged unfair labour practice on the part of the employer. The Industrial Tribunals had the right not to enquire into a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice. The appellant could not rely on r. 18 (a), and the Industrial Court had no jurisdiction to inquire into it. Parshotam Lal Dhingra vs Union of India, [1958] S.C.R. 828, relied on. The appellant had not been able to show that the discharge was mala fide. Parshotaram Lal Dhingras vs Union of india, [19581 S.C R. 828 and The Chartered Bank, Bombay vs The Chartered Bank Employees ' Union, [1960] 1 S.C,R. 200, referred to.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that it was entitled to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The suit was compromised and a fresh agreement was executed between the parties. The agreement provided that the appellant would exhibit the motion pictures of the respondent in the theatre and that the respondent would be entitled to exhibit the same in the theatre in the same manner as the appellant had been exhibiting the same. The appellant applied to the Court of Small Causes for an order that issues Nos. 11, 12 and 13 be tried as preliminary issues. The trial Judge observed that the issues were not purely of law, that in any event the case or any part thereof was not likely to be disposed of on these issues, and that the case was not likely be disposed of in the present suit. The revision application against that order was dismissed in limine by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court had no jurisdiction to record any finding on the issue of res judicata in a revision application filed against an order refusing to uphold an objection to certain question asked to a witness under examination. The true nature of the order brought before the High Court and the dimensions of the dispute covered thereby apparently got blurred and the High Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the trial Court, and which could not be decided by the High court until the parties had opportunity to lead evidence thereon. The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the proceeding in a civil court. To interpret the expression "case", as an entire proceeding only and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved litigant where it is most needed and may result In the perpetration of gross injustice. But it was not decided in Major section section Khanna 's case that every order of the Court in the course of a suit amounts to a case decided. A case may be said to be decided, if the Court adjudicates for the purposes of the suit some right or obligation of the parties in controversy; every order in the suit cannot be regarded as a case decided within the meaning of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The order passed by the High 'Court is set aside and the trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [441 D F] Major section section Khan vs Sardar Partap Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 418, referred to. The true character of the order brings it within the purview of section 115 C.P.C. The order in the present case was not a decision of the Court and that the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960 had not decided that the agreement dated March 27, 1954, was of the nature of a lease. The consent decree in the present was not a judgment by consent. The consent order was not a decree by consent. [442 B C]

The respondent was appointed as a Secretary, Zila Sainik Board, Unnao on 20.8.1979. The State Government issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military officials were appointed on contract for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme the State of Uttar pradesh appointed the respondent as the Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of Unnao in the State of U.P. The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms and conditions contained in the said order including the term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms and condi tions he was appointed as the Secretary. The respondent filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the order of termination of his service. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the order of termina tion could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be allowed. The High court further held that the termination order could not be sustain ed and the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled to remain in service. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order dated 24.3.1988 passed by the High Court in the Writ Petition did not make out that the respondent had put forward at that stage such a case. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true position that emerges from the material on record is that the respondent was employed only under a contract which specified the term of his appointment which extended only upto 30th of August, 1985. Since it is admitted that no order of extension had been sanctioned by the Governor beyond 30th August, 1985, the respondent was enti tled to the salary and allowances due to him till 30th August 1985 if the order of terminated service served on him on 29.3.1985 was found to be an invalid one. [243G H; 244A] 1.2 The order passed on review on 26.7.1988 does not make out the case that the respondent has put forward at the stage of extension such a case, and the respondent is entitled to be reinstated in service. [244B] 243 2.1 The order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court dated 26.71988 in the Writ Appeal is wholly unsustainable. The respondent had not urged before the High Court that the order was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th of 8th August, 1988 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. Even the order passed on Review on 26.3.88 does not make any out that the respond ent had put forward such a case at that stage. His only case was that the interim order that had been passed on 10.7.86 entitled him to be reinstated. [244C D] 2.2 The High Court was right in disposing of the Writ Petition on 24.3 1988 declaring that the respondent is enti tlely entitled to salary up to the period he is entitled to remain i.e. 30th August. 1985. [244E]

The appellant was tried for an offence under section 302, I.P.C. for causing the death of his wife. The prosecution case was that the appellant and his brother, the deceased, were married about one and a half years before the occurrence. The deceased gave birth to a female child in the house of the appellant. The appellant and his mother went away. The deceased and her brother, P.W. 1, went to the house of his mother in law and stayed in the house. On the next day, the appellant again requested his mother in Law to send his wife to his house. The mother and the child, according to customary practice, were taken by the mother of the deceased to her house at about 10 p.m. The appellant again came to the house and called his mother. The mother went to the appellant 's house and the appellant went away. After the deceased and her mother went to her mother in law 's house, the appellant went to the village and stayed in a house. The appellant went to his mother inlaw 's house. The deceased was found dead in the house and her body was found in the house, The appellant was charged under section 302 I.P C. and the trial court acquitted him. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the finding of acquittal and convicted the appellant under section 302. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal. The High, Court was justified in reversing the finding of the trial court. The High 'Court was also right in holding that the medical evidence supported the prosecution version and not the defence version. Merely because the medical officer stated that the victim could have received the injury if she was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have been received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused. The injury was inflicted with great force and its direction was upward. According to the accused the deceased received the injury when she placed herself between P.W 1 and himself. The injury must have been caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is true that the accused did not have any deep motive to kill his wife and that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the wife to send her with him to his house, but he probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. The Inspector of Police, P. W. 15, stated that P.W 3 did not state before him that she saw the accused making a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased. The High. Court was also right that the medical officer did not state that the injury found on the deceased could have been caused even if she was lying. The injury could have also been received in circumstances mentioned by P.W 2. The injury to the deceased was inflicted with very great force and it was not possible to say that the injury was received in the manner alleged by the prosecution. The injury, therefore, must have been received by the deceased when she was lying on the right side. The injury is, therefore, inflicted with great violence and its direction is upward. The medical evidence also shows that the injury is inflicted with great care and caution. [368C, 369A, 370B, 370F, 370H, 371A, 372A, 373A, 373B, 373C] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , referred to. 2. The High Courts should not interfere with the order 'of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. The principles are now well settled. The High courts should not interfere in the order of acquit ment merely because another views are also possible. [369B] 3. The principles laid down in Sanwat Singh 's case may be added to the principles laid down by the Privy Council in Sheo Swarup vs Emperor, A.I.R. 1934 P.C. 227. In the instant case, the High Court was justified, in interfering with an order of acquittal, because, the trial court had taken a possible view and acquitted the accused. [369C] 4. The principles to be kept in mind in the matter of appreciation of evidence are : (i) that an order of acqui sition should not be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only, and (ii) that the High Court should not interfere merely because another contrary view is possible. [368D] Sanwat 's case, A.l. R. , referred to,

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge of a High Court under article 124(4) of the Constitution. The Judge was removed from his office by an order of the President under article 124 (4) of Constitution. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of removal on the ground that the Judge was not competent to act as a Judge and that the order of the removal was vitiated by mala fides. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Judge of the High Court was a constitutional functionary appointed under article 124 and under the provisions of article 217 of the Constitution re jected the Judge on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity by an order passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority not less than two thirds of the members of that House present and voting, had been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the grounds of proved misbehavior or incapacity. The appellant contended that the power of the President to appoint a Judge of High Court under Article 124(4), read with Article 217, was to be found in article 217 and that the power to remove a Judge from his office was to be governed by the procedure prescribed in article 124(5) and that the President could not be considered as the authority to grant sanction for prosecution of a Judge under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Judge of the supreme Court and of the High Courts are constitutional functionaries. The Judge is appointed under the provisions Of article 124(1) and is removable by the President only after an address is passed by each House by a majority. The power to remove the Judge is to be found only in article 124 (5) and not in article 217. [223B C] 2. The Judge enjoys the same constitutional protection as a Judge. He enjoys the same protection as a member of the Indian Civil Service. He enjoys a constitutional protection as the Chief Justice of India. He enjoys also the same protection under article 217. The Judge holds office during good behaviour and is not removed from his post in exercise of the power of removal vested in the President under Article 124 (4). The Judge enjoys protection of the tenure of office and conditions of service as laid down in the Judges (Inquiry) Rules, 1969. [223D E] 3. The Judge, though a constitutional functionary, enjoys the same status and position as a Judge, and is entitled to the protection of the law. He enjoys protection of a judicial officer. He enjoys no constitutional protection. He enjoys constitutional protection of the Judges (Discipline and Appeal) Act, 1975. He enjoys special protection under article 124 of the Constitution and is not removable from his office in exercise of his power of removal. [223G H] 4. The Judge does not enjoy any constitutional protection. The Judge has the protection of article 217. He enjoys that protection when he is removed from his appointment by the President under the provisions contained in article 124 of Constitution. [224B] 5. The Judge cannot be removed from his Office by the President in exercise of power under article 124 unless the procedure prescribed by article 124(3) is followed. The procedure prescribed by Article 124(3), however, is not to be followed if the Judge is removed from the office in exercise or his power of appointment under article 217, and the Judge enjoys protection under article 218. [224D E] 6. The Judge can be removed from office by an Order of the President passed after an ap plication of the grounds set out in clauses (4) and (5) of article 124. [224E] 7. The procedure for investigation and proof of the misbehaviour or incompetence of a Judge is provided in article 124. The Judges (Inquiries) Rules, 1968 have been framed under section 7(4) and section 8 of the Act. The said Act and the Rules made thereunder only provide for removal of a Judge on the grounds set forth in clauses (1) and (2) of article 126. The Judges of the Supreme court and the High Courts, are appointed under the Judges (inquiry) Rules. The Judge (Inquiry), Rules, 1969 have been framed by the President to regulate the procedure for the presentation of an address and for the investigation and proof, of the misbehavior of a Judge. The Judge who is removed from office is entitled to a similar protection under article 126(4) read with article 218. The Judge enjoy the same protection of the same protection and is not entitled to the same protection in respect of any matter, even if not specified in the order of appointment. [224G H; 225A B] 8. The Judge in the instant case, enjoys the protection of a Judge of his Court and enjoys the protection and privileges of a Judge, even though he is removed by the President from his office. The Judge also enjoys the protection under article 220(2) of the constitution. The Judge enjoyed the protection of an Additional Judge of the Delhi High Court and enjoys special protection of the Judge of a Supreme Court. The Judge had the protection of Article 217. The Judges ' (Inquiry ) Rules, 1969, have been framed in exercise of this power. The Judge could be removed from the Office of a Judge by the President by an order under article 124 read with article 217. There is no reason to exclude the Judge from the protection of these provisions. [225B D] 9. The Judge 's right to a full and free trial is not impaired by the fact that he is not required to be a Judge of that Court. The right to a fair trial is not denied to a Judge. [226B] 10. The Judge must be deemed to be a public servant under section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. The Judge held office during good behavior and is not remove ed from his office under the provisions. The Judge did not enjoy any Constitutional protection. He enjoyed the protection and privilege of a Judge even though he was removed by the Government from his appointment. The Judge possesses the protection of section 21 of Indian Penal Code and enjoys the same privileges of a public servant. [226D E] 11. The Judge may be removed from service by an order made under article 124, read with article 124(6), but he cannot be removed by an order unless the procedure for removal is followed. [226E] 12. The Judge would not enjoy any legal protection. He is not entitled, therefore, to the protection under the Constitution. [226G] 13. The Judge shall not be removed from Office except in the manner provided in article 193 of the Constitution, and the procedure prescribed under article 193 shall be followed. [227B] 14. The Judge will not be removed unless he has been given an opportunity of being heard in the matter. [227C] 15. The Judge should not be removed until he has been heard in the manner prescribed in clause (4) or clause (5) or clause(6) of article 193 of Constitution. If the Judge is not removed until he is heard in the procedure prescribed for removal, the Judge shall be deemed to have been removed from his public office. [227D] 16. The Judge retains

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. He was elected to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad constituency reserved for members of the Scheduled Castes. The respondent challenged the election on the ground that the appellant was a "Scheduled Caste" and that he was not a member of the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 of the Presidential Order. The High Court held that the appellant did not belong to the Scheduled Caste, and set aside his election. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appellant was a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste group of Sahas. The respondent called witnesses to establish that the appellant belonged to the smaller group of Sahash. All the courts in West Bengal came to the conclusion that it had not been provided in the Order that the appellant had to be a "Scheduled caste" and that the appellant could not be a " Scheduled Caste" and set aside the election. [391 D] The appellant was not proved to belong, to the smaller class group of SahAS. The respondent was not therefore entitled to support the appellant 's election on the basis of the evidence in the case. [391 E] The appeal must accordingly be allowed. [392 B] The word "Scheduled Caste " in item 40, of the President 's Order, means a caste which is recognised as such by the President. The President 's order does not say that a caste is a caste. The President has power to specify castes or tribes by public notification. [391 C] The expression "Scheduled Castes" in item 40 refers to castes. If the intention was to exclude from the caste group those members of that caste who bore the surname Saha, the item would have said so; it would then have read "Scheduled Castes". [391 D E] The appellant 's case that he belonged to the Saha caste was not proved. The evidence led in a case may be imperfect. Suppose the evidence in another case led to the conclusion, as it might conceivably do, that there was a smaller caste group within the Saha caste group of which the appellant was the Saha caste, the court could say that the appellant ' was a "Sikh" and not a "Scheduled Castes", and that the expression "Scheduled Caste meant a group within the Sunri caste". [391 F G] The appellant must be held to belong to a Scheduled Caste specified by item 40 of that Order. [392 A] The respondent called witness to establish that appellant belonged to a smaller caste. All the Courts in West Bengal, therefore, came to the conclu sion that it had no been provided in this case that the appellant, belonged to the larger caste group of Saha caste. [392 C]

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay, which belonged to a lady named Durgeshwari Devi. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It was said that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the complainant through one Sayed for the purpose of making necessary ar rangements about the flat occupied by him in view of his intended departure. The prosecution case was that the accused demanded a sum of Rs. 30,000 which was later reduced to Rs. 29,500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs. 2,000 for the furniture and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The complainant actually paid the accused two sums of money on 7th November, 1948 and 17th November,1948. He, however, got into touch on 1st December, 1948, through one Sayed, for the purpose for making necessary arches. The complainant and a Sub Inspector of Police, who was down below ready for the raid, held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement for transfer of the gas connection to the name of the complainant. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, LVII of 1947, for receiving a pugree of Rs. 29.500 and he was further charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relinquishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appellant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat, that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complainant, and that the sum of money was not pugree but represented capital for 0 12 0 share in the business and as the com plainant was also to be a caretaker of the flat, the sum of the money was paid and received as a guarantee against disposal and damage of the furniture and it was agreed to be paid back on the appellant 's return to India. The Presidency Magistrate, who tried the case, dis missed the defence on the facts, holding that what was received by the accused was by way of pugree. As section 18(i) of the said Act was not applicable he convicted him under section 19 (2) of that Act and sentenced him, in view of the old age and blindness, to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 100. The wife of the appellant filed an appeal to the High Court of Bombay but it was summarily dismissed on 20 2 1950. The appellant applied for special leave to appeal to this Court and it was granted on 3 10 1950. The question for consideration was whether the offence under section 19 of the Act arose on receipt of any sum or any consideration as a condition of the relinquishment by the tenant of his tenancy of any premises. Held, that an assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction. It is the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt of consideration that has been made an offence. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. The consent to the assignment is not required in the case of relinquishment or surrender of tenancy. The consent is not necessary in the case where the tenant disappeared from the scene altogether, saying nothing and making no arrangement about his interest and possession under the lease. The consent given by the landlord to the transfer is not necessary. The consent must be to the relinquishment of the tenancy of any property by the tenant. The consent may be given by the tenant or by the landlord but the consent must be given by a consent of the tenant or the landlord. The consent by the landlord is not necessary where the tenant is dead and his heirs are not living. The consent cannot be given by one of the parties to a transaction. The consent can be given by any one who holds his interest. The consent in the present case was given by the appellant and the appellant was not a consenting party to the transaction. The appellant had not given his consent to the transaction and the conviction under section 19 was not sustainable.

The appellant, a public limited company, was engaged in the manufacture of aerated water. The company had a wage scale of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ per month. The company was making good profits in the year ending 31st March, 1976. The company, however, had to pay a salary of Rs. 5/ per month to its employees. The company claimed that the existing wage scales should be revised to Rs. 150/. The Tribunal, however, held that the existing wages should be revised with effect from 1st January, 1976. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the Tribunal should have fixed the dearness allowance in the revised wage scales, that the Tribunal was wrong in taking the rise in the cost of living index as a criterion for fixing the wage scales, and that the Tribunal had committed an error in taking the flat increase of Rs. 100 as the basis for fixing the dearness allowance. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right in holding that the existing dearness allowance should be revised in the wage scales with effect from January 1, 1976. [181 B] 2. The Tribunal has relied on the statement of the appellant that a flat increase of the wage scale was intended to be given to each workman in addition to the benefits conferred by the revised pay scales and other awarded reliefs. The Tribunal had not taken into account the fact that the appellant had to pay the increased dearness allowance to its employees in the category of Draftsmen and of the other categories. [181 C D] 3. The Tribunal, in the present case, considered the matter and found it sufficient and in accord with justice that the wage scales should he restructured with suitable increments provided therein. [181 E] 4. The award of the Industrial Tribunal was a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments, longer span of 20 years for earning increments, dearness allowance at 10% of the basic wage, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial capacity of the appellant. It is needless to recapitulate all the basic facts which have been set out in the judgment of Pathak, J. The Tribunal considered the matter, and found it necessary to revise the wage scales. [181 F H] 5. The award is a composite document. It is not possible to accept the contention that the Tribunal committed an error of jurisdiction in taking the view that the flat increase to the pay of each workman was intended to each of the employees in the categories of Draftsman and of Rs.100/ and of Rs 100/ respectively. [181 G H] 6. The Tribunal did not take into account the basic fact that the company had to pay increased dearness allowance of Rs. 10/ to its employees and that the company was not entitled to claim the increased dearness pay. [182 A] 7. The Tribunal erred in taking the increase in the cost price of living index. The Tribunal should have taken the increase in cost of living as a criterion. [182 B] 8. The Tribunal committed an obvious error in taking into account the rise in cost of wages of the employees. The Tribunal ought to have taken the rise in wages of the workmen as a criterion, and not the rise in dearness allowance. [182 C] 9. The Tribunal failed to take into account that the company could very well bear the additional financial burden. [182 D] 10. The Tribunal also erred in taking into consideration the fact that a flat increased in the case of the category of Draughtsmen and the other categories was not regarded as an addition to the pay. [183 A] 11. The Tribunal wrongly assumed that the company would be entitled to claim a flat increase in the case Of Draughtsman and the other category. [183 B] 12. The Tribunal overlooked the fact that in the case where the company had a gratuity scheme, the company had been paying a gratuity scheme. [183 C] 13. The Tribunal ignored the fact that there was no evidence that the company paid a gratuity scheme to its employees, and that it was not possible to say that the company did not pay a gratuity scheme in the case. [183 D] 14. The Tribunal took into account the circumstance that the company made a provision for a gratuity scheme and that the scheme was not likely to be more beneficial than the scheme of the gratuity scheme. The Tribunal could not have taken the flat increase as a criterion of the revision of the wage scales and the flat increase in wages. [183 E] 15. The Tribunal misdirected itself in taking into the matter the rise in price of living. The Tribunal adopted a flat increase which was not regarded by the company as an addition in the case, of the other category of workmen. [183 F] 16. The Tribunal in the present ease, considered the question of revision of the pay scales and flat or ad hoc increase of salaries of workmen wherever considered necessary. It cannot possibly be doubted that an Industrial Tribunal deciding upon the wage scales of the employees of an establishment would have full liberty to propose ad hoc increase in salaries as part of the revision in wages. Nor can it be doubted that fitment into the revised pay scale is certainly a part of the revised pay. [184 B C] 17. The award was a composite award in which the various elements of increased wages, larger increments and longer span of service for earning increments were integrated into a balancing arrangement in keeping the wage scales in view. [184 D] 18. The Tribunal rightly held that the present company can bear the additional burden. [185 E] 19. The Tribunal 's decision that the existing pay scales should be restructured was not based on any irrelevant consideration. The Tribunal made an error in its approach by taking the flat rise in the case as a criterion and not the increase in dearness allowance, and by taking the rise as a criterion in the case which was not accepted by the company. [185 F G] 20. The Tribunal went wrong in taking into accounts the fact that an increase in the price of living was not a criterion for revision of wages. [186 A]

The respondent, an employee of the appellant, was charged with an offence under section 14(1)(d) of the , for having refused to pay to him the wages of his employees. The appellant contended that the wages prescribed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages under section 2(vi) of the Act, and that the applications made by the respondent were incompetent under section 15 of the Act. The Industrial Tribunal, which was constituted under the , made an award fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day and in pursuance of the said award, the appellant paid its employees only Rs. 10/ per day. The respondent contended that the appellant was not entitled to recover the said amount as it was not a part of the terms of the contract of employment, and that, in any case, the applications made under section 15 were incompetent under the section. The appellant 's contention was rejected by the Industrial Tribunal. The High Court affirmed the finding of the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The wages prescribed by an award cannot be treated as wages under section2(vi) before it was amended. The amended definition of wages, in section 2(v) of the Industrial Disputes Act, does not apply to the present case. The terms of employment have always been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Therefore, the basic assumption made by the appellant that section 2(vii) cannot take in the wages prescribed in the award, is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structure prescribed by the Award. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. [422 D F] South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, A.I.R. 1951 Cal. 29, approved.

The appellant was a Sub divisional Officer in the service of the State Government. He was charged with criminal misappropriation of a sum of Rs. 51, which was the amount drawn by him from the State Government by way of salary. The prosecution case was that the appellant had received a sum of about Rs. 51 from the State. The appellant denied the receipt of the sum and pleaded that he had paid it to the khalasi. The trial court convicted him under section 409 and section 409 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court, on appeal, held that the prosecution had failed to establish that the amount drawn was paid to the appellant by way of remuneration for the services rendered by him. The appellant contended that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for his prosecution under section 409. Held, that the prosecution was not vitiated by the absence of sanction under section 9(1) Of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, as the appellant had not been charged with the offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery. The appellant was not charged with the commission of criminal misappropriation of the amount. The appellant had not received the sum from the State, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there was in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. The appellant did not claim to have paid the amount to the klalasi. The appellant could not be prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Code of Criminal Proce dure. The acts with which the appellant was charged were official acts and the prosecution was bad for want of sanction under the section. Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor, (1939) L.R. 67 I.A. 372, distinguished. The appellant 's conviction was illegal. The appellant received the sum of Rs 51 from the khalashi and he admitted the receipt of it. The acquittance rolls were not produced in the trial court. The appellant, therefore, could not be convicted under section 409, Indian Penal Code, as the prosecution had not established that the amount was paid to him by way of gratification. The appellant should be acquitted. Hori ar Singh vs Emperor (1939] L.R., 67 I. A. 372, referred to. The appellant must be acquitted. The conviction of the appellant was illegal. Hori and Ram Singh vs King Emperor, (1948) L. R. 75 I. A, 180, distinguished. Hori Lal Singh vs Emperor , referred to. Hori Raj Singh vs Emperor [1939] I.L.R. , distinguished. The question whether sanction under section I7(1) was necessary for the prosecution of the appellant under section 409 was not a matter which was relevant at the stage of sanction, as the acts with which he was charged were not such as could be justified by him as done by virtue of his office.

The appellant, a bank, was carrying on business at its head office in Cochin State and it carried on business in the State of Cochin and also in the State in which it was carrying on its business. The appellant was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 51 under the Travancore Income tax Act, for the assessment years 1950 51 and 1951 52. The appellant claimed that the loss incurred in the State was a loss of business in the Travancore State and was entitled to deduct the loss from its profits under section 32(1) proviso (1) of the Travancore Income Tax Act, and the first proviso to that section was applicable to the case. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the appellant being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduction of the losses incurred outside the Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that State. The Tribunal also did not accept the appellant 's contention that the loss in the State could be deducted from the profits of the Travancore State. The High Court, on a reference, held that the loss under one head of profits or gains was allowed to be set off against income, profits and gains under any other head and that the first proviso was a modification of the method of computation under section 10(2) of the Indian Income tax Act for determining profits and gains of the business of any resident. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the words " business or vocation " in section 10 of the Indian income tax Act, 1922, must be construed in the context of the main enactment and the context of its own provisions and the words " loss of profits or gain " in the proviso must be construed to mean loss of profits and gains arising in an Indian State. The use of the words " a loss of profits " in the main enactment is not sufficient to restrict the scope of the proviso to the business alone. The proviso to section 24(1) of Travancore Income tax act, 1125, is to be construed harmoniously with the main enactment. The word " business " in the context in which it occurs in section 10(1) must be construed as meaning " business in British India or business in an Indian state" and the words must be construed not in their technical sense but in their ordinary sense. The words " business " and " business " must be construed together and the context in section 10 (1) must show that the word " business" in the context is not used in the narrow sense of business in British Indian or business in any Indian State or so divide business. The use in the proviso to section 10(i) of the Act of the words loss of profits to be set of against business in British india or business in Indian State and the use in the main provision of the proviso of the words, " where the loss sustained is a loss of profit or gains " in the first proviso, indicate that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising in Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under the section. The proviso is not to be construed as a proviso to the main enactment but as a proviso only to the main provision. The words used in the proviso are " a loss " and not " loss of profit " and the use of the word " loss " in the second proviso to section 14(2) (e) and the use " in the third proviso to section 15(2) are not sufficient to limit the scope of that proviso to business alone. In re: Mishrimal Gulabchand, , In re: Raghunath Parshad, and In re: The Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, Bombay, , referred to.

The respondent company was incorporated in January, 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July, 1947, the private limited company was converted into a public limited company. The head office of the company was at Calcutta. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices was to retire its employees at the age of 55. In September, 1959, an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 60. Shortly after this the company 's employees at Bombay raised a dispute regarding their retirement age. The Tribunal directed that the age of superannuation should be 58 but the company may in its discretion and with the express or implied consent of the employee continue an employee after he attained that age. The company 's appeal to this Court was against the decision of the Tribunal. HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that the age fixed by the company should be 58. The Tribunal had found that in all the awards in recent years in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix the age of retire ment at 60. But on a closer examination it was clear that this document was of little assistance for finding out the recent trend. There was no indication at all as to how long ago the age of 58 was fixed at 55 or at 58. The statement filed by the workmen to explain this Chart showed that in two of these cases, viz., Ingerzoll Band and Northern Assurance Co., the demand for fixing the age of re servation at 60 years was under negotiation. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding the age of the workmen to be 55. [428 B D] Imperial Chemical Industries (India) Private Ltd., vs The Workmen, ; , referred to. Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; and Dunzell vs Union of India, ; , distinguished. The Tribunal considered it to be its duty to enquire whether the conclusion recorded by this Court in some of its earlier decisions was accurate. Having embarked an this enquiry, the Tribunal took considerable pains to perform this duty and it had ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. [429 B C]

The appellants, who were the shareholders of a company, were the directors of the company. The Board of Directors of the company, in exercise of its powers under section 237(b) of the , made an order on May 19, 1965, that the affairs of the company be investigated by a Board of Company Law Administration consisting of a Chairman and a member. The order was challenged by the appellants on the grounds that (1) the order was made mala fide; (2) that in making the order the Board had acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(a); (3) that the order having in fact been made at the instance of the shareholders was invalid and on a true construction of section 237 this could not be done; (4) that the Board had not acted on material, extraneous to the matter mentioned in section 235(a); and (5) that the impugned order was invalid because it was made by the Chairman of the Board and not by the Board. The High Court rejected the contentions and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The order made by the Board on May 19. 1965, was not made mala fide or is otherwise invalid. The Board had not made any order under section 237 (b) mala fide or otherwise. The order did not amount to a finding of fraud. [327 B] (2) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237(B) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board is administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman, of the Board by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Government under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the company; that the opinion to be formed under section 237 is subjective and that if the grounds are disclosed by the Board the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. [327 C E] (3) The order dated May 19,1965 was passed by the Chairman on behalf of the Board. He was not a member of the Board but was a member of a committee. The Chairman was not a delegate of the Board, and the Board could not delegate its function under section 237 to the Chairman. [327 F G] (4) The Board of Company law Administration consists of a Chairman, a member and a Chairman. The Chairman is appointed by the Central Govern ment by a notification under section 237. The Board is not a body corporate. The Chairman has to be appointed by the Government. The Board has to function under the control of the Chairman. The Board can delegate its functions to the Chairman or any other member of the board. The Chairman cannot delegate his functions to any other member. The Board cannot delegate its functions except with the consent of the Chairman, and the Chairman cannot delegate the functions except with his consent. [327 H] (5) The power under section 237 can be exercised by the Board independently of any rules framed by the Central government. The Central Government had under sections 10E(1) and 642(l) ample power to frame rules authorising the Chairman to distribute the business of the Board to the Chairman and to control the Board in the exercise of its delegated functions. The power under sub section (4A) may be exercised by a Board independently of rules framed by that Government. [327 G H] (6) The Central Government has power to constitute the Company Law board and to delegate its functions. [328 B] (7) The power of the Central Government to make an order under section 639(4A) is not violative of article 14. [329 C] (8) The power to make an interim order under section 235(1) is not discriminatory. The power to appoint an inspector under section 237, is not discriminatory and is not violative Of article 14. The power is not discriminatory because the power to appoint inspector is not discriminatory, because the power is not absolute. [330 C D] (9) The power is conferred on the Board to distribute the work of the Board among the members of the Board who are the members of a committee constituted by the Board under section 10E. The power can be exercised only by the Board and the Central Government. The Central Govern ment has power to appoint a committee to investigate the affairs of a company in different sets of circumstances and the power can be delegated to the Board. [331 C D] The Central Government could not delegate the power to the Chairman to sub delegate the function of the Board under the Act to the Chairman, because the Board could delegate its functions only to the Chairman who was a member. [332 E] (10) The power given to the Central Government is not discriminatory as the power to make the order under section 23(4A), is not discriminatory in that it is not made by the Central Govt. but by the Board itself. [333 A] (11) The power can also be exercised by an authority not authorised by the Act. [334 B] (12) The power could be exercised by any authority not authorised to act under the Act. The Central Govt. had under sections 237(b), 237(c) and 237(d) power to appoint inspectors and to make investigation. The power could also be exercised under section 237 by the Central Board or the Central Government or by the Central Gov ernment. [335 B] (13) The power cannot be exercised by one member of the body. The power may be exercised either by the Board or by the Chairman. If the power is exercised by one of the members, the power cannot be delegated to any other. [336 C] (14) The power may also be exercised in the absence of any statutory provision. [337 C] (15) The power must be exercised by authority which is authorised to do so by the Act and the rules. The power cannot, therefore, be delegated to a member of an authority. [339 C] (16) The power, under section 237 could be exercised only in the absence, of any statutory provisions. The power must, therefore, he exercised by the authority which is competent to do so. [340 D] (17) The power was not discriminatory because, the power to delegate to the Chairman was not discriminatory. [341 E] (18) The power in the present case was not discriminatory as it was not made by any statutory provision but by the Act itself. [340 F] (19) The power has been exercised by the Central Govenment under section 237 and the Central Govt has been empowered to appoint inspect ers and to make inquiry. The power has not been exercised by any statutory authority. [340 G] (20) The power should be exercised by such authority as the Central Government may specify in this behalf. [340 H] (21) The power does not suffer from any defect. [341 A] (22) The power delegated to the Chairman is not discriminatory since the power to determine the question of the existence of circumstances which led to the formation of the opinion is vested in the Central Government and not in the Chairman. The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/ each. The High Court, and the Court below, drawn from this the conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and convicted them accordingly under section 395. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The law advocated by the appellants was not correct. If there was other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of the stolen property with him was a piece of evidence which connects him further with the crime. There was no question of presumption. The evidence was only to be taken as to be sufficient to connect the appellants with the crime, and the presumption was stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime was made immediately after the crime was committed. [723 B C] The presumption to be drawn ought to have been one under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act or at the most under section 412 of the Indian penal Code but not of complicity in the crime of dacoity. [724 B] The evidence was not sufficient to connect appellants with the offence of dacoity. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the stolen goods were found in their houses. It was impossible to think that these 20 persons were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits. It was legitimate therefore to raise the presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. [725 B C] 723 The fact that the goods were recovered from the possession of the appellants was a piece piece of evidence to connect them with the crime and the presumption under section 114 was drawn. [726 B]

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'thinner ', 'thinners ' and 'thin sets ', were carrying on business in the State of Delhi. They were prosecuted under section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (hereinafter called 'the Act ') for importing 'thiners ' and 'tins ' from abroad. The trial court convicted them and sentenced them to various terms of imprisonment. The High Court dismissed their appeal. In the petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, the petitioners contended that the Act was a Central enactment and that the State Government could not exercise its power under the Act, as the Act was not applicable to the State of Punjab. Dismissing the petition, the Court, HELD: 1. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances were included in the Rules made in 1926 as poisons and that is not in dispute. Section 5 of the Act deals with presumption and states that any substance specified as a poison in a Rule or notifica tion issued under the Act shall be deemed to be a poison for the purpose of the Act. Rules of 1926 were made in exercise of the rule making power under section 3 of the Act, which enables the State Government to make Rules generally to carry out the purposes and objects of the Act and Rules were amended in 1973 and duly notified as required by the Act. Section 2(3) of the Act defines 'poison ' as: "any substance which are applied to the body or to the body by means of any chemical or other device, and which, either by itself or in combination with any of these, is capable of producing a poison, whether in the form of a powder, grafted or otherwise or by means of a mixture of any two or all of such substances. " Section 4 of the Act impliedly sets out certain guidelines when the State can notify a substance as poison. It states that the State Govern ment may by rule regulate the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which the use of such poison for the purposes of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to it to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the posses sion thereof desirable. Any substance which is used for purposes mentioned therein can definitely be declared as poison. That is what the Government have done in this case. It has become a notorious fact, which is notorious, which is also a fact that the substance known as 'thiner ' as it is or mixing with some other substances are taken as intoxicating spirits endangering the life. In many cases death has also occurred due to drinking such substance. If the Government thought in the circumstances that the posses tion or sale of the same is to be regulated it could not be said that they have no power to regulate. Section 2 also enables the Government by Rule to regulate the possession for sale and the sale of the specified poison. It is in exercise of this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old Rule by the following Rule: "13 (1) All poisons kept for sale by any licence holder under these rules (except those kept by a chemist, druggist or compounder for the purchase of dispensing or compounding in compliance with the prescription of medical or veterinary practitioner) shall be kept in a box, almirah, room or building (according to the quantity maintained) which shall be secured by lock and key and in which no substance shall be placed other than poisons possessed in accordance with a licence granted under the Act and each poison shall be kept within such box, altar or room. Every such box, box, al fort or room shall be marked with the word "poison" in red charac ters both English and vernacular and in the case of receptacles containing separate 'poison" with the name of such 'poison". "Provided that this rule shall not apply to 'poison " mentioned in clause (x) of Rule 2. " The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu lish the possession and sale in that area. No question of discrimination can arise in such circumstances. The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. The writ petition accordingly fails and it is dismissed. [225D F]

The appellants were partners of a firm which carried on money lending business. The firm was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1952 53. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim of the appellants to a certain sum of money as bad debt on the ground that the transactions were mere accommodations which could have no bearing to the regular business carried on by the appellants. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The Tribunal, however, held that the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending business not a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. The High Court, on a reference, answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Tribunal has not raised any inference from the circumstances and has merely observed that charging of interest cannot make it a money lending account. The statement of the case is intended to be a finding on facts and not a catalogue of the arguments advanced at the bar. [419 D] (2) The statement of case submitted by the Tribunal is inadequate. It contains only a summary of the business relations between the appellants and the Bombay firm, a statement as to the amounts due at the end of each year at the foot of the account, the interest if any charged and a summary of orders made by the Income tax officer, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. [419 E] (3) The statement is not a catalogue. It contains merely a summary of business relations between. the appellants and their partners. The failure to adjust interest in the account of the Bombay firm at the stage at which it became a debtor in the Samvat year 2007, the manner in which the partner of the appellant firm tried to explain the position in March, 1954 and the stand of the firm itself at all earlier stages support the case of the Department. [419 F G] (4) The Tribunal had found that the monies sent by the appellants to the Bombay firm were not loans made in the ordinary course of money lending business, nor in respect of any other business of the assessee. The Tribunal had also found that the moneys sent by the appellant to the Bombay firms were not loans. [419 H] (5) The Tribunal was right in reframing the question referred to it. [420 B] (6) The Tribunal, in the circumstances, was right in holding that the debt in question was not a debt in the assessee 's money lending business nor a debt representing a loss sustained in other business. [420 C] (7) The Tribunal found that the money sent by the assessee to the Bombay Firm was not loans made by the assessee in the ordinary, course of its money lending. The finding of the Tribunal was supported by the evidence on record. [420 D] (8) The Tribunal 's finding that the monies were sent by the Bombay firm was not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. [421 B]

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The awards were made on September 20, 1984. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984, with which we are not directly concerned here. The said Special Leave Petition was dismissed on April 29, 1987. The petitioners filed writ petitions challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards were not made within the stipulated time. In these writ petitions, the Karnataka High court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. These petitions were dismissed by a Single Judge of that High Court on November 29, 1988. Appeals against the decision of a Single Judge were dismissed by the Karnataka High. The petitioners preferred Special Leave Petitions against the decision in the Special Leave Petitions. The petitioners contended that as the awards in these cases had not been made within two years of the notification making the declaration under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Petitions and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [565E] 2. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosing of the same definitely amounts to suppression. [566A] 3. The interim stay orders have a clear bearing on the non disclosure and the non furnishing of the same. [567B] 4. The interim order has a direct bearing to the question raised. [568B] 5. The interim Orders have a direct impact on the question of the acquisition. [575C] 6. The fact that the stay orders were obtained by the petitioners by practising fraud on the Court is of no consequence. [585D] 7. The interim Order has a direct impact and a material change in the circumstances. [587D]

The appellant, a public spirited citizen, had filed a writ petition in the High Court of Calcutta challenging the constitutional validity of the West Bengal Land Reforms and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1981, which was dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. The appellant filed an appeal before the Division Bench of the High court which was also dismissed. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the decision of the Government to lease the land to the appellant was arbitrary and unreasonable and that the Government had no power to transfer the land to a hotel. The appellant also contended that the Government was not justified in taking over the land from the appellant without inviting tenders and that the land could not be leased to the appellant without the tender. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The public interest litigation is based on the ground that the decision to lease the Government land to the petitioner was arbitrary and that the decision was arbitrary and was not based on relevant considerations. The persons or authorities in whom the Government has a share or interest are and must be parties to the dispute. But the normal meaning of the word "public interest" is a matter of public interest. [277E G] 1.3 The Government is not and cannot be a private litigant but a public spiri ture litigant. The Government is answerable to the people. The Government cannot act like a private litigant in the field of land revenue. The Government has to pay the land revenue to the State. The Government can also not allow the use of the land to other purposes. The Government may use the land for any purpose other than those for which it is granted. The Government also cannot lease the land or lease the superstructure. The Government, however, has to pay a certain amount to the person or persons who have constructed the superstructure on the land. The Government could not be a private party to the dispute between the Government, and the person who constructed the super structure. The Government was not and could not be the owner of the land. The Government must be held to be a model litigant. It is not only the interest of the Government which is being affected but the interest of justice which requires that the Government should be held to have acted fairly and reasonably.
