The workmen of the appellant company claimed sick leave for 7 days with full pay and dearness allowance in a year, with the facility of accumulation upto 21 days. The company contended that the benefit of the sick leave was available to them under the Act. The Tribunal awarded 7 days sick leave with full pay, and dearness allowance to the workmen of that company in a year with the facility for accumulation upto 21 day. The award was on the lines of the earlier award in the case of the Alembic Glass Industries Ltd. The workmen of the Aldechares Ltd. also filed a statement containing information regarding the companies which had provided the benefit of sick leave to its workmen in the region. The company also allowed 6 days sick leave in a year to its employees in Bangalore and it was permissible to accumulate it upto 12 days in addition to the current year 's leave, under a settlement dated July 17, 1969, which was being continued even after the coming into force of the Act. In the case of Jyoti Ltd. Baroda, the Tribunal awarded 7 day sick leave with half pay and dearness pay in a year. The workmen also filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of the Act were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969 and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The benefit of sickle leave was lost when the Act was made applicable to the region from December 14. 1969. The Tribunal could not be said to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were getting under the award of 1958, for it was taken away under the mistaken impression that it had been adequately replaced by the new provisions on the coming into operation of the Act, and the workmen were entitled to 7 days sickle leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. [86D E] The Act does not in fact deal with the question of sickness leave. The other question regarding the adequacy of the sick ness benefit under the provisions of the Act has been examined by the Tribunal with reference to the reports of the National Commission of Labour, 1969, the Labour Laws Review Committee and the Norms Committee of Gujarat State, which go to show that the benefit cannot be said to be adequate for it works out to about half the average wage of a workman, and even that amount is not admissible for the first two days of sickness except in the case Of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which the sickness benefit was last paid. [86F H] The Act came into force in the region concerned on December 14,1969, and it has not been disputed that till then it was the practice in the glass industries to grant sick leave with wages for periods varying from 6 to 10 days. In fact in the case. of the A.I.L.M.S. Ltd., Baroda, the award for 7 days sick leave on full pay and. dearness allowance in 1958, subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the Act became available to the workmen. The benefit of the. sick leave was therefore lost when the A.L. M.S. Act was made applica ble to the region. [86H; 87A B] The Alembica Chemical Industries Ltd. vs Its Workmen and others, [1969] 1 S.C.R. 107, referred to.

The appellant was detained under the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1947. The grounds of detention were supplied to him on the 8th June, 1955, and the order of detention was passed on the 8.6.1955. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the order of the detention was mala fide, (2) that the detaining authority in passing the order of 8.6 was acting at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan Action Committee, and (3) that the grounds of detention supplied to the appellant were vague. Held, that the order was not mala fide and that the detention was valid. The constitutional right of a detenue under article 22(5) of the Constitution comprises two distinct components. The right to be furnished grounds of detention as soon as may be and the right to be afforded the earliest opportunity of making a representation against his detention (1) ,184. 391 are vested in the detaining authority, not in any other. The authority is under a constitutional obligation to furnish reasonably definite grounds, as well as adequate particulars then and there, or shortly thereafter. But the right of the detenue to be furnished particulars, is subject to the limitation under article 22 (6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. The duty to consider whether the disclosure of facts involved in the grounds is against public interest, is not a duty to disclose facts considered to he against public interest. The authority to furnish particulars is not a judicial tribunal. The duty of the detaining authority to consider whether or not the disclosure of any facts involved in grounds is against the public interest, cannot be implied. The authority must be under a constitutional duty to furnish reasonably the grounds of the order of preventive detention. The authority was therefore under a constitutional obligations to furnish reasonably particulars of the grounds of preventive detention and the duty to consider the question of disclosure of facts, which is a statutory obligation, cannot be delegated to the detaining authority. The fact that the detaining officer did not make any application to the Government to be supplied with particulars of the ground of detention, cannot be held to be a ground of detention which could be considered to be vague. The fact of non disclosure of the facts as well as the ambit of the non disclosure must be clearly communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds are furnished. The non communication of the decision not to disclose particulars is not fatal to the constitutional right of the detenu. The fact, that the detaining 'authority did not make a claim in the affidavit that it was claiming privilege or applying its mind to the question of privilege, is not an unreasonable restriction on the right of a detenu to be afforded a proper opportunity of representation. The fact in the present case that the detaining. authority did not make an application to the State Government to be furnished with particulars of grounds of detention, could not be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate the decision not disclosed to him. The fact could not be said to have been considered by the detaining authority at the time of the making of the order. The fact was not disclosed to the appellant at the time the order was made. The fact did not amount to a denial of the right of making a proper representation. The order was not therefore bad. The State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya, ; , referred to.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. He committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were that he was a member of a party to a party to which he was a party. The respondent was called upon to submit his explanation by way of defence. The explanation of the respondent was placed before the Central Government. The Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory and on April 9, 1959, an order was passed removing the respondent from service. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. The High Court allowed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appeal must be allowed. The power under section 19 of the read with r. 14 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words "subject to the provisions of this Act", it speaks of removal of a person from the service. Rule 14 is such a rule : it is, therefore, not ultra vires. [450 D] The words "subjectto the provisions of the Act" occurring in section 19 of Act, are, therefore, mutually exclusive. The result is that r.14 of the Army Rule, 1954, is not ultra vires the . [450 E] The appeal must accordingly be allowed. [450 G] The appeal is allowed. The case will now go back to the High Court for disposal on merits on the other questions raised by the respondent in the High Court. [450 H] The case will go back to High Court for hearing on merits on other questions raised in the High court. [450 A] The case is remanded to the High court for disposal on other questions. [450 B] The case must be disposed of on merits.

The appellant was a Panchayat constituted under the Bombay Village Panchayat Act, 1958. The Panchayat passed a resolution on June 1, 1959, imposing octroi duty on goods coming within its local limits as per the Schedule No. 1 of the Rules. The resolution was approved by the Collector. The Panchayat filed an appeal under section 124(5) of the Act before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Panchayat Samiti rejected the appeal by its resolution dated September 4, 1963. While the appeal was pending the Panchayat passed a Resolution No. 3 on January 26, 1963, fixing octroi limits and number of octroi nakas and their places. The Panchayat wrote to the Collector seeking his approval to the octroi limits, number of octroi posts and places. The Collector approved the octroi limits and the number and location of octroi naka within the limits of the jurisdiction of the Panchayat under r. 21 of the Fees Rules. The Panchayat then filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court held that the Panchayat Samiti could not dismiss the appeal as being barred by limitation because r. 5 of the Fees Rule was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. The High court also held that the octroi duty was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. The High, Court did not deal with the question whether the company 's tea was imported into the limits of Panchayat for consumption, use or sale because it felt that sufficient facts had not been found by the Standing Committee. The High. Court felt that it would not be proper to determine facts for itself. The High 'Court felt that it was not proper to determine the facts for itself and that the approval of the octroi limits on January 14, 1964, related back to April 1, 1963. The High Courts order was set aside and the case was remanded to the High Court to deal with the case on merits. The Panchayat appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the Panchayat could validly impose octroi duty from January 14,1964, in accordance with the resolutions dated February 25, 1963 and March 17, 1963. [217 B] The rules which authorised the imposition of octroi were framed under section 176 of the Act. The rules were framed under the Bombay Panchayat Act, and the rules were framed in exercise of the powers conferred by section 176(1). The rules were not confined to octroi duty only. The rules did not require the Panchayat to fix the tax in the resolution passed under r. 3(a). The resolution was passed by the Panchayat in exercise of its powers under section 176(2). [217 C D] The rules were made in exercise of powers under section 175(2) of the Bombay Panchayat ' Act. The resolution of the Panchayat was passed in exercise of those powers. The rules are not confined to the imposition of tax only. The resolution could not be said to be ultra vires the rules. [218 B] The High Court had rightly held that the resolution of the panchayat was not ultra vires. [218 C] The High Courts ' order was set 'aside and the case remanded to the Panchayat for disposal on merits. [218 D] The High court was right in its view that the Panchayat was entitled to proceed with the appeal on merits.

The conciliation proceedings were pending when the appellants were dismissed. The appellants were convicted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1) of the Act and sentenced to a fine of Rs. 250 and the appellants were acquitted. The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings should be held to terminate when the Conciliation Officer is required under section 12(6) of the , to submit his report but the provisions of the Act above quoted do not support this contention. Held, that the conciliation proceeding should be held in the present case to terminate when a report is received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings were not concluded when the report under section 12 (6) was received by the Government. The con stitution of conciliation proceedings under section 12 of the Act does not affect the pendency of the conciliation proceedings and if for some reason the Conciliation Officer delayed the submission of his report his action may be reprehensible but that will not affect the interpretation to be put on section 20(2)(b) of the . Workers of the Industry Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the Industry Co. Ltd., ; , followed. Held, further, that the termination of the conciliation proceeding was not a continuation of the conciliation proceed ings and the conciliation proceedings were therefore not terminated when the report was received by Government. The proceedings were not terminated when a report was received under section 12, and the conciliation proceeding could be prolonged much beyond what was contemplated by the Act and the termination would depend upon how soon a report is made by the appropriate Govern ment. Held, also, that the con stitution and the conciliation proceedings were not terminated by the con sion of the Conciliation Officer and the con stitu tion and the termination of conciliation proceedings were in law deemed to take place when the report is received.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The District Magistrate, Dhanbad in respect of the petitioner under section 3 (2) of , on the ground that the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The petitioner 's representation was rejected by the Government. The petitioner challenged the order of detention in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order of the detention was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated by the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. In the instant case when the actual order of detention was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There was no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. If there were cogent materials for thinking that the detenu might be release then these should have been made apparent. [911B C] 2. The order of detention, though justified when it was passed, was not invalid and on relevant considerations the service of order was not on proper consideration. [912B] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Burdwan & Anr., ; ; Ramesh Yadav vs District Magistrate Etah & Ors., ; ; Raj Kumar Singh vs State of Bihar & Ors., Crl. A. 353/86 with Crl. A 353/86, dt. 26.9.86, referred to. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the continued detention of the detenu under the Act is not justified. [910B] 3. The order is set aside. The writ petition and the appeal are allowed to the extent indicated above. [913C]

The appellant, a dealer in gold, was carrying on business as a money lender and a goldsmith. The Administrator of the Union of India, exercising powers under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968, refused permission to the appellant to carry on money lending business on the ground that the appellant was carrying on money lending and was, therefore, not entitled to the permission. The High Court, in a petition under article 226 of the Constitution, struck down the section on the ground of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guidelines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary, uncanalised power upon the Administrator with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on the money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that section 28 of Gold Control Act is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [955 B C] (2) The object of the Gold (Control) Act is to control the production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and to prevent circumvention of other provisions of the Act. The policy and the scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of that Act afford more than sufficient guidance to Administrator in the exercise of his discretion under section 28. [956 B C] Harakchand Banthia vs Union of India & Ors. ; , followed. (3) The High Courts have upheld the validity of section 28 of Act. [959 D] (4) The analogy drawn by the High Court from the reasoning adopted by this Court in Harakchand Bantharia 's case is not applicable to the instant case. [951 E] (5) The High court has rightly held that the section does not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lenders, banking or any other business in the same promises in which he carries on business as money lenders or banker on the security Of any article, ornaments or both unless authorised by the Administrator. Even the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on business, as a money lenders banker or any other person in the same 'premises is not absolute in as much as the Administrator can authorise the third person to carry on business in the licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy and purposes of the Act and by the prime consideration that circumvention of provisions of the other sections of the Act shall not be premitted. [952 B C]

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for a declaration that the properties in suit belonged to the temple and for possession of the same. The trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the properties belonged to the trust and that the appellants had failed to prove that they had acquired title by adverse possession. The lower appellate Court held that the appellants were entitled to the properties in question. The High Court, in appeal, held that the properties were not liable to be treated as properties of the temple. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. The questions that fell for consideration were : (i) whether the properties in the suit were granted to the temple by the then Ruler of the State of Travancore Cochin, and (ii) whether the appellants had acquired title to the properties by adverse possession, and whether the suit was barred by article 134 B of the Indian Limitation Act. HELD : (i). The properties in the present case were granted to a temple by the Ruler of the erstwhile State of Travancore. The properties were granted to an idol and its manager. The properties had been granted to the deity and its manager as absolute owners. The properties did not belong to the temple but to the appellants. The properties belonged to a temple and to the deity. The properties, therefore, were not granted to the idol but to the deity, and the appellants had no title to them. [7E F] (ii) The appellants had failed in proving that they had been removed from the office of the manager of the temple by any of the previous managers. The appellants had not proved that the properties had been transferred by the previous manager for valuable consideration. [7G] Vidya Varuthi vs Balusu Gurulingaswami, I.L.R. , referred to. (iii) The appellants ' case that the properties did not belonged to the idols was not proved. [7H] (iv) The appellants were not entitled to the benefit of article 134 B, because, the properties belonged not to the idoli or temple but to a temple. [8A] (v) The appellants could not succeed in the present suit on the basis that the properties fell within the purview of article 134B, because, article 134 B applies to all cases where it is shown that the immovable property was comprised in the endowment and that it has been transferred by a previous manager for a valuable consideration. The successor has to prove three facts : (1) that the property belongs to the religious endowment; (2) that it was transferred by a new manager; and (3) that the transfer was for a valuable considerations. [130B C] (vi) The appellants have failed to prove the existence of any temple in the temple. [130D] (vii) The appellants did not prove that the properties have been transferred by any of previous managers for valuable consideration, and the suit was therefore barred by article 133 B. [130E] (viii) The appellants failed to prove their title to the suit properties. [130F] (ix) The appellants claimed title to the property on the basis of adverse possession. [130G] (x) The appellants contended that the suit was not barred by article 132 B, because the suit was brought by the next friend of the appellants, and not by the previous friend, and that the suit should have been dismissed on that ground. [130H] (xi) The appellants cannot succeed on the basis, that article 132 B applies to the facts of the present case. [130C] (xii) The appellants are not entitled to succeed on the ground that the suit is barred by article 136. [130A] (xiii) The appellants must succeed on the strength of the decision of the Privy Council in Vidya Varti 's case. [131B] (xiv) The appellants do not claim title to the temple on the basis either of title or of adverse possession, but they claim title to a temple on the strength, of the title of the manager. [131C] (xv) The appellants, therefore, have failed to establish that they had become entitled to the property by adverse possession and that the property was not liable to vest in the temple under article 134 B. [131D]

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the orders passed by the District Magis trate and the appellate authority. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant came up in appeal to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The licence granted to the appellant was for running the Theatran tation. The licence is for the premises permanently equipped for cinematograph exhibition in the name and style of the Theater. The appellants were displaced persons from Pakistan and were granted lease of certain mills and the factory in question. The respondent issued a notice to the appellants, under section 12 of the (XXXI of 1950), of the evacuee property in respect of which directions were given under section 10 of the Act, and called upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not be evicted. The appellants contended that section 12 of Act XXXI of 1950, which applied only to leases granted by the evacuee, and not by the Custodian, was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under that section. Held, that the Custodian had the power under section 12 to cancel a lease granted by himself and not by a Custodian and that the notice, Exhibit C, was ultravires the powers of section 12. The Custodian had the authority under section 12, to cancel a leases granted by himself, and not the Custodian, and the notice, therefore, was valid. The Custodian bad the power under the section to cancel leases granted by him, and the notices, Exhibit C and Exhibit C, were valid. The section, as it stood at the relevant time, did not apply to leases granted before the amendment of the section, and the Custodian had no power to cancel them. The section was not intended to affect the powers of a Custodian to cancel leases, and did not affect the powers conferred on him by the section. The section could not be construed as cutting down the plain meaning of the operative portion of the section. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, ; , referred to. The section did not confer any authority on the Custodian to go back upon his own contracts. The operative portion of section 12, as it then stood, was unqualified and absolute, and that power could not be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The section could be construed as conferring no authority on the custodian to go back on his own contracts, and the section could not therefore be construed as giving him authority to go back by a mere contract. The section cannot be construed as taking away the powers of an evacuee to deal with his property, and the words "notwithstanding any law for the lime being in force" in the section must be construed as meaning that the Custodian could not go back upon the terms of the lease, and that the Custodian was entitled to cancel the lease.

The appellant was a minor son of the respondent. The respondent filed an application before the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, for determining the ceiling area of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer determined the ceiling area, but an appeal by the respondent was allowed by the Revenue Appellate Authority. The Board of Revenue in revision, however, remanded the case to the Sub Divisional officer for fresh determination of the ceiling area. The Sub Division Officer, Hanumangar, by his order dated 5th May, 1976, held that the father and the son constituted two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Bighas and 8 Biswas. The Sub divisional Officer, therefore, held that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order of the Sub Divisional Offi cer and, consequently, set aside the order of Sub Divisional Officer dated 5th may, 1976 and remanded the case for fresh determination. The Sub Divi sional Officer, Hanumagarh, by his orders dated 6th September, 1976 and 6th September 1976, held the appellant and his son as entitled to retain 124 Bighas and 16 Biswas only and the surplus land measuring 4 Bighas and 6 Biswas may be resumed. The appellant filed an appeal before the Revenue Appellate 626 Authority, Bikaner, who by his order of 6th September. 1976 dismissed the same and upheld the order of sub Divisional Officer. The appellant then filed a revision application under Section 230 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 before the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan. The Board by its order dated 14th April, 1975 remanded the case back to the Sub divisional officer for fresh disposal. The Sub divi sional Officer, Hanumbargarh, by order dated 5.5.1976, held that Surendrapal Singh, the appellant, was born to the respondent on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional offi cer. He further held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub Divisional Magistrate had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling 925 area under the new law i.e. the Act of 1973. The Board, therefore, set aside that part of the Sub division 's order which had gone against the State and in favour of the appellant, and remanded the matter to the Sub Diviional Officer, Bikaner for fresh determination on the basis of the old law. The appellant 's revision application under section 230 of the Act was dismissed by the Board of Reve nue on the ground that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. The appellant challenged the orders of the Board of revenue by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Board has general powers of superintendence and control in respect of all revenue courts. It is open to the Board to exercise its powers of superintendence on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of the subordinate courts so as to keep them within their spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to Board of Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. [726C D] 2. The Board had by its order of 14th April 1975 directed that the ceiling area may be determined according to old law i. e. Act of 1955 and it spite of it the Sub division officer committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Board. [728B] 3. The Board in its order dated 4th April 1975 had not gone into the merits of the controversy nor had it thought it advisable to do so. The Board was, therefore, not justified in remanding the case to Sub divisional Magistrate for fresh determination by him. [729C] 4. The Board did not go into the merits nor did it think it advisable to examine the controversy nor did it go into the question whether the appellant was entitled to retain the land in dispute. The Board could not, therefore, have decided the controversy nor could it have given its finding on the question of the appellant 's right to retain the disputed land. [727D] 5. The Board also did not go in the matter into the merits or the controversy nor was it inclined to go into the matter. The Board merely remanded the case. The Sub divided officer was, therefore. not justified in remitting the case to him for fresh determination and the Board was not justified in setting aside the order dated 5 5 1976 of Sub divisional magistrate. [730B C] 6. The Board 's order dated 4 4 1975 was not based on any legal or factual basis. The Board should have gone into the matter and decided it in the light of the observations of the Board and the Board 's orders. [731B] 7. The Board committed the grave error of law and acted in excess of its jurisdiction in remanding the matter to Sub division ers. [732B]

The first respondent, All India Reporter Limited, was not served with any individual notice by the Tribunal before it passed its award. The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court questioning the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur, calling upon it to implement the orders of the Central Government on the basis of the recommendations of the Palekar Tribunal. The High Court accepted the plea of the first respondent and declared that the law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and that the demand made by the Deputy Commissioner to comply with the order made by the Central Government was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. Aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, the appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the first respondent are reports of recent decisions of the Supreme Court of India and of the High Courts in India which are supplied to it by its agents appointed at New Delhi and other places where High Courts are situated. It cannot be disputed that these decisions are of public importance. Article 141 of the Constitution provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. Even apart from Article 141 of Constitution, the decisions of the superior courts while they settle the disputes between the parties to the proceedings in which they are given, they are the sources of law in so far as all others are concerned. [780D E] 779 2. The first Respondent, All India Edition of the Indian Express, is a newspaper and the other publishers of law reports in the interests of their own business vie with each other to publish the judgments of the Supreme Courts or of the High courts as early as possible in their law reports which contain information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. Strong reliance was placed on behalf of the first Respondent on the decision of this Court in P.S.V. Iyer vs Commissioner of Sales Tax, Orissa, AIR 1960 Orissa 221 in which the question that arose for consideration was whether a law journal, a law report published from Calcutta, a law journal published from Calcutta and a law journal in Calcutta were newspapers within the definition of the expression "newspaper" in section 2(c) of the . [780F G] 3. The law reported which are being edited by the first Respondent contain information about recent events which are matters in the Supreme Courts and the High Courts are the highest courts of the land. The law journalists are interested in knowing the contents and the effect of the decisions. The first responder, All India Journalists, is a journalist and the other respondents are its editors. The law report published by the respondent contain information about its recent decisions which are matters of public importance and the High Court of Bombay declined to follow the decision of that High Court in Commissoner of Sales Tax vs M/s. The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. The respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. The appellant was a tenant of the premises since about two years. The respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that the appellant was a licensee and not a tenant. The trial Judge passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st January, 1975. The appellant filed an appeal against the said decree. The appellant contended that he was a licensee. The respondent contended that there was sub tenancy by the respondent in favour of the appellant as a monthly tenant. The appellant also contended that the Court of Small Causes had no jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition in this case. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was a licensee, that there was no sub tenancy by him, that the Court had no jurisdiction and that there was a bar to the jurisdiction of the Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent was a monthly tenancy of the suit property since about two and a half years. The appellant had agreed to pay rent at the rate of Rs.225 per month. The agreement recited that the licensee shall not allow any other person to use and occupy the said premises and shall not do any unlawful or illegal business therein. The agreement was only for the purpose of paying rent at the agreed rate. The agreement did not create any interest in the premises. The agreement also stipulated that the licensee would be entitled to keep the keys of the premises with him and that he would work in the said premises for twenty hours subject to restriction of rules and regulations imposed by the Municipal or any other local authority or authorities. The agreement further stipulated that the appellant would be entitled only to keep the key of the premises in his possession and that he was at liberty to work in the premises for twenty four hours subject to restrictions of rules and regulation imposed by the municipal or any other authority. The agreement stipulated that the licensor would be entitled at his option to terminate the agreement by giving one month 's notice. The agreement provided that the licenee would be entitled for the period of the agreement to keep the premises in good repair and to take all necessary repairs. The agreement, however, stipulated that the respondent would be entitled not to remove himself from the premises but to remove himself and his belongings on the expiry of the agreement or sooner termination or determination thereof after deducting all the dues if any for payment of compensation. The agreement mentioned that the licecer would be entitled, on the licensee surrendering possession of the premises, to keep the possession of the said premises with him. The agreement clearly stipulated that the licencee would not allow any one to use and occupation of the said property and would not do any illegal or unlawful business therein. It was also stipulated that he would not do anything which would be repugnant to the terms and conditions of the agreement. The agreement in question was a lease and not a licence. The respondent was not a licensee. He was not a tenant of any premises. The respondent had filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the suit properties. The appellant 's suit was decreed. The respondent preferred an appeal against that decree. The High court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. The High, Court affirmed the decision of the trial court that the respondent had a licensee and that he could not be evicted from the suit premises. The High. Court held that the respondent could not be said to be a licensee. It was further held that the agreement was a lease. The High Courts decision in D.H. Maniar and Anr. vs M/s. Bright Bros. (Pvt.) Ltd. and Ors., [1987] 2 S.C.C. 394, was not applicable to the facts of the case. The appellant, therefore, did not get the advantage of the amended provision of the Bombay Rent Act. The respondent in that case had filed a revision petition under section 115 of C.P.C. in the High Court. The High 'Court refused to interfere with the finding of the Small Causes Court that the respondent 's possession was not lawful. The High [1065B C] 10. In the instant case, the agreement in question read as a whole was lease and not licence. The High was right in holding that the respondent did not get any right to continue in possession of the property after the expiry of his agreement. The High had rightly held that the appellant had not got any right to remain in possession after the expiry or termination of his agreement and that the respondent continued to be a tenant. The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of former Dholpur State into the Matsya Union. The United State of Rajasthan ultimately became the Part B State of Rajasthan on January 26, 1950. The United States of Rajasthan merged with the Matsya union in 1949. The United states of Rajasthan and the Matsya Unions merged in 1949. In 1949 the United State of Rajas than merged in 1949 and the Matsyas were merged in 1949, but the United State was not bound by any obligation against the old sovereign of the former State of Dholpur. The United state of Rajasthan was a new sovereign and was not bound to refund the amount due to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for refund of the amount. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but the first appellate court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The respondent was not entitled to the refund of the amounts due to it. The United St ate of Rajasthan was not bound under article 295(2) of the Constitution to refund the amounts due. The liability of the State of Rajasthan under article 295 (2) of Constitution was not to be confused with the liability of the former Ruler of Dholpur. [180 D] The United State was a new Sovereign and was not liable to refund the money due to the respondents. [180 E] The liability of a Ruler of an Indian State to pay taxes or duties was not to he confused with the obligation of the former ruler to pay the taxes or duties. [180 F] The United States was a new State and was not a party to the Covenant entered into by the Ruler of Dholpur with the Ruler of the United State. The United was not bound either by the Covenant or by the Covenant to refund the tax or duty. [180 G] The United states were not bound to pay the tax or duties to the respondent as the Ruler of an erstwhile State merged with the United States. [180 H] The United India was a new Government and was not responsible for the payment of the tax or customs to the respondent, and the respondent was not bound. [181 B] The United United State of Matsya Union vs The United States, ; , referred to. The United United States was not bound in the present case to refund the taxes or customs to which the respondent was entitled. [181 C] The United Provinces vs Atiqa Begum, ; , applied. The United India had no right to the refund claimed. [182 A] The United Province vs Atiqat Ali, ; , relied on. The United Provinces was a new Ruler and was not subject to the liability of refund of tax or customs. [182 B] The respondent was therefore not entitled to recover the amount of tax or custom from the United States of Matsya. [182 C] The respondent could not be allowed to recover the amounts of tax or duty from the United states of Matsya, because, the United states were bound to refund such amounts to the respondent under the Covenant entered by the Ruler with the United states. [182 D] The respondent had not taken the plea that the liability of payment of tax or of custom was not recognised by the United States and was not enforceable against the United states, and the United states could not be made liable for the amounts of the tax and custom. [182 E] The United, United States was also not bound to return the amounts of customs duty and customs to the United states because, the respondent was a new ruler and was not entitled under the Covenant to recover the tax or custom duty from the U.P. State. [182 F] The respondent would be entitled to recover from the United State the amount of customs duty or customs duty which it had paid to the United States, but the respondent would not be entitled to claim refund of the customs duty or custom duty paid to the U. P. State because, the U. U. State was not a part of the United States at the time of merger. [182 G]

The appellants, who were the owners of cotton and groundnut oil mills, challenged the constitutional validity of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, which provided for the establishment of markets for the purchase and sale of commercial crops. The Act was passed to provide for the better regulation of the buying and selling of commercial crops in the State of Madras and for that purpose to establish markets and make rules for their proper administration. The Act provided for the constitution of a market committee for the purchase, sale, storage and processing of commercial crops and for the establishment and constitution of market committees for the regulation of the purchase, and sale of such crops. The State Government issued a notification under section 18 of the Act declaring its intention to exercise control over the purchase and selling of such commercial crops. After the issue of the notification, the State Government issued another notification under section 19 of the Act directing that the provisions of the Act and the Rules and Bye laws framed thereunder shall apply to the purchase and sales of commercial crops specified in the notification. The appellants challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds, inter alia, that the Act and Rules were invalid as they contravened the provisions of article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution of India. Held, that the provisions Of the Act and rules made thereunder were not invalid on the ground that they contravened article 19(i)(g) Of the Constitution. The Act and the rules were not invalid merely because they were made under section 18 Of the Act. The Act did not create unreasonable restrictions on the appellants ' fundamental right to do business. The restrictions imposed by the Act and by the Rules were reasonable restrictions within the meaning of article 19 (6) Of the constitution. The Act, therefore, was valid. The Act imposed reasonable restrictions on the right of the appellants to carry on their trade and business and the restrictions imposed by it were reasonable within the meaning Of article 19(6) Of Constitution. The restrictions were not unreasonable restrictions and could not be held to be unreasonable merely because they did not carry out the object for which they were enacted. The Act in question was an integrated one and it regulates the buying and sale of the commercial crops. If the small traders were exempted, it created to them a monopoly to trade in the notified crops and the Act was not intended to interfere with that right. The Act could not be said to create unreasonable restrictions. The Act had been enacted to provide for better regulation of buying and selling and for the regulation and control of the buying, selling and processing of the commercial crop. The Act is an integrated one, and it regulises the buying and the selling of commercial crop. If the petty traders were exempted from the operation of the Act, the Act would be invalid as it would be inconsistent with the provisions of section 14 Of the Act which prohibits the deduction of trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances. The deduction of 'maii ' as trade allowance was not a trade allowance within the meaning section 14 Of Act. The deduction was not a deduction from the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, but a deduction from price or commodity settled by the market committee for its own use or benefit. The deduction could not be justified as trade allowance. The deduction would be a trade allowance for the purpose of the Act. It was not a payment out of the price or the commodity agreed to to be paid, but a payment for the purpose or use of the premises or services rendered. The deduction may be out of the commodity or out of the money agreed to be given or transferred, it would be a payment out, of the price. The question whether a particular payment is a trade allowance or not depends upon the facts of each case. The deduction must be in any transaction in respect of commercial crops, and if it is a deduction out of the market or market established, it would not be a deduction from, the price or in any transaction. The deduction is not a deduction for trade allowance within section 14 Of Madras Act III of 1933. The Act does not create unreasonable restriction on the appellants fundamental right to carry on trade or business. The Act imposes reasonable restrictions on their right to do trade or business and the restriction imposed by it was reasonable within the terms of article 19 of the Constitution. T. B. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority, Tanjore, ; , Ramunni Kurup vs The Panchayat Board, Badagara, ; and Captain Ganpati Singhji vs The State of Ajmer, ; , referred to.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellants contended that the conviction was bad as the High Court had not given any reasons for its decision. Held, that the conviction of the appellants was not bad. The High Courts have the power to dismiss an appeal in limine where the decision appealed from is one of conviction and sentence and not of conviction and the sentence is one of death. The powers of the Supreme Court under article 136 of the Constitution are very wide and the Supreme Court does not interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the High Court. The Supreme Court does interfere with the sentence passed by the High Courts in appeal if the High Court has not followed the procedure prescribed by law or has acted perversely. The Supreme Courts does not interfere in appeal against the sentence passed or sentence passed by a High Court. In the present case, the High Court did not give any reasons for the decision of the appeal. The Supreme ' Court does not ordinarily interfere in appeal under article 136. The Supreme, Court does not exercise its power under article 136 where the High Court, in the exercise of its discretion, has not followed certain procedure or has acted in violation of the principles of natural justice. The Supreme. Court does not act as a court of appeal in the exercise Of its powers under article 136 and does not act merely as a court hearing an appeal under article 134(1) (c) of the Constitution. The Supreme court does not exercise the power of an appellate court under article 136 when it is dealing with an appeal against the order of conviction and sentences passed by a criminal court. The Supreme 905 Court does not function as a court to hear appeals against acquittal and the Supreme Courts do not function as courts of appeal in criminal cases. The Supreme .Court does not function in the exercise 'of its power under Article 136 where the Supreme Court is hearing an appeal against an order of acquittal and the High Court is hearing the appeal against the confirmation of the sentence. The Supreme; Court does not entertain an appeal against a sentence passed by High Court in the exercise or its power of enhancement under article 136, and does not exercise any power of an Appellate Court under article 134 (1) (a) of the constitution. The Supreme Appellate Courts do not act as courts of first appeal in the matter of awarding of sentences. The Supreme Supreme Court does function as a Court of appeal in its power of superintendence under article 136 (1) of the Constitu tion and does not entertain a petition for enhancement of sentence. The High. Courts do not exercise the powers of an appellate Court under article 226 of the Constitution and do not act in the exercise, of their power of superintendence. The Supreme ,Court does not entertain any appeal against the orders of conviction and, sentence passed by, the High Courts. The Supreme High Courts do not entertain any petition for enhancement in criminal cases where the High Courts have not followed the provisions of section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Supreme the High Courts do entertain petitions for enhancement of sentences and do not exercise any powers of an Appellate court under article 226. The Supreme and the High Courts are not courts of first instance in the matter. The Supreme is not a court of first appeal under article 133 of the Constitution, and the Supreme 'Court does not exercise power of an appeal under that Article. The Supreme are not courts in the exercise and exercise of their powers of superintendence under articles 136 and 136 of the constitution and do not entertain a revision petition against the orders passed by the Supreme Court. The High, Courts do not interfere in revision under article 136 against the orders made by the High courts in exercise of their power under article 226, and do not interfere with sentences passed by the courts below in exercise of the powers of enhancement under section 401 of the Code. The Supreme The High Courts do exercise the power under article 227 of the Constitution in revision against the orders and sentences passed in exercise of its power of revision under article 227. The Supreme ;The High Courts do. not exercise the jurisdiction under article 136 in the matter, of enhancement of sentence and do not deal with the case in exercise of that jurisdiction. The Supreme has the power to revise the orders of the Supreme. Court under article 32 of the Constitution under article 136(1) of. the Constitution.

The petitioner was employed in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 made under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged the order of compulsory retirement in a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The writ petition was dismissed by a Bench of this Court on the ground that the petitioner was an officiating Government servant and could not have been compulsorily retired under Rule 56 (j) of Fundamental Rules. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner was holding a class II post when the impugned order was served on him. The petitioner had not at tained the age of 35 years. As already indicated, he had crossed the age of 50 years but had not attained the age of 55 years by the date of the order. Therefore, sub clause (1) was not contravened when the order was made. It has been argued before this Court that as the petitioner was holding an officiating appointment in Class II service, he could not have compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). [638C D] 2. The petitioner has not attained the 55 years age by the date the order was passed. The appropriate authority is entitled to exercise power under clause (j) in the case of a Government servant in Class I or Class II service or post where he entered into service before attaining the age of 30 years after the said servant attained the age o f 50 years. [638E F] 3. The petitioner is entitled to salary and other service benefits payable to him from the date of compulsory retirement till the date of his normal superannuation. [639B] 4. The petitioner would have superannuated from service on 29.2.1980 if he had not been compulsorily retired with effect from 6.5.1976. Even if the writ petition is allowed and the order of compul sory retirement is set aside the petitioner cannot go back to service. But he would be entitled to pecuniary benefit of salary and allowances admissible under the rules. [640B C] 5. The petitioner will have superannuated from serv ice on 29. 2.1980 if the petitioner had not been compulsory retired with effect fram 6.5,1976. [641B] 6. The petitioner shall be paid salary and other allowances payable to him for the period between 5.11.1976 and 29.2,1980. [642B]

The policy had two clauses, clause (1) provided that the policy was to be in force for a period one year from the date of its commencement. Clause (2) provided that if the policy was not renewed for one year, the policy would be deemed to have been cancelled and the sum insured would be payable to the nominee. The trial court held that the proposal must be accepted by the Divisional Manager and that the appellant had not filed the evidence of any orders prohibiting other officers, one step below, in this case the Assistant Divisional Manager to exercise the power of Divisional Manager. The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of money against the appellant. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant applied for a certificate under article 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution. The High Court granted the certificate. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appeal was not maintainable since the decision on the issue did not finally dispose of the dispute between the parties. The order appealed against was not a final order within the meaning of section 109(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure or section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935, if it amounted to a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in the suit or proceeding; if after the order was made, the suit or proceedings still remained to be tried, and the rights in dispute had to be determined, the order was interlocutory. [702 C D] Ramchand Manjimal vs Goverdhandas Vishindas Ratan Chand, L.R. 47 I.A. 124, Abdul Rahman vs D.K. Cassim & Sons, L. R. 60 I.A, 76, Mohammad Amin Brothers vs Kesho Prasad Singh, L.I.A. 76, Abdul Rahman 's case, L.L.R. 60 I A. 76, Mohammad Amirul Hassan vs Abdul Rahman, L. L.R., 60 I. A. 76 and Mohanlal Thakkar vs D. K. Cassinar, C.A. No. 7 of 1958 dt. 10 10 59, referred to. The Federal Court in Mohanlal Thakkar 's case held that an order was final within the meaning Of article 133 of the Constitution, under section 109 Code of Civil Proce dure or section 205 Code of Criminal Procedure, if it amounts to final decision on rights of the par ties in dispute in a suit or proceeding, if after the decree is made, the proceeding in the court of first instance, and the proceeding for filing a complaint under section 476 of the Code, are a self contained proceeding and were finally disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complaint under s. 205 read with section 114 I.P.C. The proceeding instituted on the complaint was not part of or incidental to the proceeding for an enquiry whether a complaint should be filed. If it did not, and the suit or proceed was a live one, yet to be tried the order was not final. Different tests have been applied, however, to orders made in proceeding independent of the original or the main proceeding. [703 C E]

The appellant was appointed as a clerk by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu, in 1963, long before the Amending Act came into force. He was, therefore, entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961, the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayat. The fact that the appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974, or the further fact that he was appointed as Head Clerk on April 1, 1975, could not improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973, being the date on which the Amending Act of 1973 came into force, and that the Panchayat Samiti had lost its power. The fact, that the appellant, was promoted as Head Clerk in January 1974 could not improve the position for the obvious reason that these were made after the Amending Act had come into force. [737E G] The fact that he had been appointed as a Head clerk on April 1. 1975 could not improve him for the simple ground that these appointments had been made after June, 1973, when the Amending Act was in force. [735A B] The fact, however, that the appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head Clerk was made after June. 1973, could not, therefore, have made any difference for the simple reasons that these appointments, were made after that date, being the day on which the Panchayat Samiti was lost. [736B C]

The property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo. On his death, the Mahant was succeeded by his son, the first respondent, who executed a will in 1956, and it was provided that the properties in the temple and the deity shall be managed by the Mahant and his son. The first respondent filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute was his personal property and that he was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The suit was contested by the first respondent. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that the property was owned by the Mahant. The High Court allowed the appeal by the first defendant and held that the property had been purchased by the first plaintiff in 1921 from the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor. The High court held that the first plaintiff was in possession of the property as Mahant and the first defendant was in possession as a trustee. The High. Court held that the fund from which the property was acquired constituted the personal property of the Mahant and did not belong to the Math or the deity. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in the view that the Amauli properties constituted the personal properties of the Mahant. On his. death in 1917, all those properties and wealth devolved on the Mahant and the son. The fund from which Amauli property was acquired was the personal property. The Mahant was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge in respect of the two fixed deposits made by the Mahant in the Bank of Bengal. The Mahant had also inherited the personal property from his father. The High, Court was right that the fund was held by the Mahant for the purchase of the Amaul properties. The fund passed to the Mahant on his death in 1917. The Mahant executed a will and it was contended that the fund passed to him on his death. The High 'Court was right in holding that the fund had been purchased in 1921 from personal funds inherited by the Mahant from his predecessor and that the fund must, therefore, be regarded as his personal property. The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They were allotted certain lands in the State of Punjab. The lands were allotted to them under the notification of the Government of Punjab dated March 24, 1955, under section 12(1) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The appellants applied to the Custodian General for the cancellation of the allotment of the lands in their favour on the ground that the lands were not available in the village Raikot. The Custodian General rejected the application on the ground, inter alia, that the jurisdiction of the Custodian General to cancel the allotment of land in the village was taken away by the provisions of section 12 of the Act. The appellants moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Custodian. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the Custodian General had no jurisdiction to cancel the order of allotment of land made in favour of the appellants. The powers conferred by section 19 of the Act on the managing officer appointed under the Act are in conflict with those conferred by section 10 of the Act and the latter cannot prevail over the former. The powers of the managing officer are confined only to properties which are entrusted to him for management and not with respect to any other property. The rule of the former is in Chapter X headed "Payment of compensation under section 10 of Act" and deals with a transfer of property to an allottee by way of final settlement of his claim to compensation and does not deal with the question of allotment on a quasi permanent basis. The rule applies to a proceeding before an authority created by the and not to an authority created under the Act. There is no substance in the argument that there is no entrustment in fact of the property or that the class of properties to which the appellants belonged continue to be evacuee properties. The appellants had lost their possession before the publication of the notification and were thus not entitled to the protection of the section. The Custodian, by reason of the divesting of the property, had become functus officio with respect to it and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation of allotment. The rule is in Chapter XI headed "Ppayment of compensation under Section 10 of the Punjab Act" and does not apply to the present case. The rule does not restrict the powers of the Custodian in the matter Of cancellation of allotment in the sense that it permits cancellation only on certain specified grounds and, therefore, it cannot be said that section 19(1) is completely in conflict with section 10 of that Act. The rule cannot be said to be in conflict with r. 102 of the Rules framed under the Act and is not applicable to the present proceedings. The rule only applies to a case where the managing officer or managing corporation is appointed under the and not where the managing corporation is constituted under the Act, and the rule does not apply where the managing committee is constituted under a statute. The rule has no application where the managing committees are constituted under a special statute.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of Boys Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) in the Uttar Pradesh Educational service Junior Scale (Junior Scale) in the Junior Scale in the Junior scale in the Junior and Senior Scale. The advertisement was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examination was over, on the basis of the results thereof, success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the written examina tion were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Commission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of it. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that the High Court was wrong in upholding the decision of the Public Service Commis sion to re hold the recruitment examination. On behalf of the respondents it was contended: (1) that the High court was right in upholding the action of the Public service Commission to cancel the recruitment examination; (2) that the recruitment which is now to be re done by completing the interview examination should be finalised within four months hence; and (3) that with the dismissal of the special leave petitions the selection of the two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates has become final and would not be disturbed. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examination and drive the candidates to litigation. [126G] 2. The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis Of the written examination. [126H] 126 3. The recruitment which is to be re examined by completing the interviews should be finalised in four months hence. [126F] 4. There shall be no order as to costs. [126B]

The appellant brought a suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State, and that he, as mahant in charge of the Shiromani Dera at Landeka, had the right to manage the properties attached to the Dera at Nanga Lakhn Kheri in the former Patiala State and that the appellant was entitled to be in possession of the properties. The appellant contended that the Dera was an independent Dera and that he was in possession of properties of the Dera as its lawfully appointed mahant. The trial court decreed the suit. The decree was reversed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit on the death of Som Dass, since there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahants to succeed him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The suit was for possession and management of the Deran Dera and the properties appertaining to it by the appellant purporting to be the de jure mahant against Som Dass as de facto mahant, and the fact that it was after Som Dass died that the appellant, as the de jured mahant was elected to be the mahant of the Dara Dera can make no difference when we are dealing with the question whether the interest in Dera devolved upon him. [489 B C] (2) The subject matter of suit was the interest of Som Dass in the Dera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as mahanta of the Dari Dera. [481 B] (3) The suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto trustee. [484 D] (4) The subject property was the interest in a representative capacity of the de facto trustee and the appeal was not competent against the de jed trustee. [490 E] (5) The subject of the suit was the right of the de jked mahant to manage the property and the properties of the de hant. [490 F] (6) The subject was the interest and interest of the dejure trustee. [491 B] (7) The subject is the interest of the person who was the de jendor of the Dana and its properties. [491 C] (8) The subject in the suit was not the interest of a de jked trustee. [492 C] (9) The subject suit was for the possession and management by the de jended trustee of the Dersara Dera and properties appertaining to the same. [493 D] (10) The subject, in the suit, was the interest, of the de emed trustee. The subject matter was the interest which was the subject matter in the suit and the interest was the interest that was the subject of the litigation. [494 E]

The appellant assessee is a dealer in raw materials and is registered as a dealer under the Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessee purchases raw materials from registered dealers and sells them to the State Trading Corporation (S.T.C.) and the State Trading Corpo ration. The assessee is also registered as a purchasing dealer under the Central Sales Tax Act. The assessee claimed that the raw materials purchased by it were "goods" within the meaning of section 2(i) of the Central Sales tax Act and were exempt from tax under section 5(1) of the Act. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee and levied purchase tax on the raw materials. The assessee 's appeals to the Assistant Commissioner and further revision to the Sales Tax Tribunal were dismissed. The High Court, however, allowed the assessee 's revision petition. The assessee contended that the words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) above were not compre hensive enough to include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than by way of sale as for example, by way of stock transfer. The Revenue contended that the goods might have been directly moved by the assessee to a port for shipment abroad in pursuance of an export contract entered into by the dealer who purchased from the assessee. The assessee, on the other hand, contended that the sale of the manufactured products by the assessee was not a sale in the course of export but was a sale in pursuance of a sale by the dealer to a foreign buyer. The High Courts, however, held that the words 'disposes of ' used in clause(a)(ii), later, clause(b) and clause(c) of section 9(1) were not restrictive of the meaning of the words 'sale by him in the course or export outside the territory of India ' and that the exemption under section 9(i) was to be restricted only to sales made in the course o export within the meaning section 5(i). The High Court held that the assessee was entitled to an exemption from the impugned purchase tax only if the sales were export sales within the meaning Of section 5(l) of the C.S.T., Act which they, admittedly, were not. The High court held that the sales to S.T. C. were inter State sales chargeable under section 5 (1) of C.S., Act and that the assessee ' 's purchases of raw materials were not liable to tax under section 6 of the Act, and that the sales of the manufactured product by the assessee were not exempt from tax. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The words "or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by sale in the con stitutional sense" in section 9(l) (b) of the Haryana General sales Tax Act,1973 are not restrictive of their meaning and are not restrictive in their application to the sale of goods in the course Of export outside the Territory of India. [362B C] 1.2 The expression "disposes off" in section 5(3) of the General Sales Tax is not restrictive of its meaning. The expression "deposes off" is used in the sense of "disposes" of the goods in the State itself. [362D] 1.3 The expression "exports out of the territory of the State of Haryana" in section 6(1) (b), which is the only provision in the Act, is not restrictive. [362E] 1.4 The expression "sale by him" in section 2(1) is not restrictive and is not restrictive in its application. [362F] 1.5 The expression "goods" in section 3(i) is not used in the narrower sense of "goods which are actually in the State at the time when the contract of sale is made". The expression "imports" is used to describe the goods which are in the State when the contract is made. [362G] 1.6 The expression "brass" in section 4(1) means "brash" or "style". [362H] 1.7 The expression "in the course of inter State trade" in section 8(1) and section 9(2) of the is not restrictive but is extensive in its application and is not restricted to "in the State of origin". [362B] 1.8 The expression "export out of the State" in section 10(1) includes "bringing into the State" also. [362C] 1.9 The expression "turnover" in section 7(1) refers to the aggregate amount for which goods are sold and not to the value of the goods which have been sold. [362H; 363A] 1.10 The expression "taxable goods" in section 12(1) which is the charging section is not restricted only to "taxable goods sold" but also to "taxable events". [362E F] 1.11 The expression "taxes on the sale or purchase of goods" in the context of the General Clauses Act, 1897, means "any tax on the sale of Goods" and is not confined to "taxes levied on the sale" of Goods.
