The expression used in section 2 of the Central Act is "for the, purpose of" and not "for sale in the Stale of Haryana". [363D] 1:18. The expression, "in the Course of export out" of the Territory means "in the immediate, direct and immediate" of the exportation. [363E] 1:19. The expression `in the course ' in section 5 (3) of General Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976 is not "in the same State" and is thus not "in course of export outside the State". [363F] 1:20.

The appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1953. The sales tax authorities assessed the appellant to purchase tax on the ground that the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The appellant contended that the sales in question were exempted from sales tax under article 19(1)(f) of the constitution. Held, that the sales tax authorities were right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of article 286(i)(b) and that the sales must be held to have taken place in the course of export out of the territory of India. The appellant was not a registered dealer and the sales were not exempted from tax. The appellant 's intention was that the goods should be exported to a foreign country and the goods should pass to the buyer at the time when the goods cross the customs frontier. The intention of the parties that in compliance with the requirements of cl. 5(2) of the Exports (Control) Order the goods shall be the property of the licensee at the time of the export would mean nothing more than that the property in the goods shall pass immediately before the ship going beyond the territorial waters of the country, or at the earliest when the ship leaves the port. The appellant had not sold the goods to the buyer in the course Of export out of India and the sales must therefore be held to be exempted from tax and the appellant was liable to purchase tax under section 10(b) of Bombay Sales Tax. The appellant could not be assessed to purchase tax in respect of the castor oil which it sold to others. The appellant did not sell the goods to a person who was not a dealer in the goods. The appellant sold the goods in the course 822 of export out Of the territory of the country and the sales tax was therefore rightly levied. The appellant therefore was not entitled under article 19 (1)(f). The Sales Tax authorities were right, in the circumstances of the case, in holding that sales tax was leviable on the appellant. The appellant should have been assessed to purchase Tax under section 10 (b) of Act. The Sales Tax Officer was therefore right in holding the appellant to be liable to purchase Tax. The Bombay High Court was right in holding in favour of the Sales Tax authorities. The Bombay Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1953, section 3, section 4 and section 5 of the Bombay Sales tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 1953, are valid and the Sales Tax Officer had jurisdiction to assess the appellant to tax under section 5 of Act. Held, further, that the appellant 's contention that the certificate of the intention of the appellant to sell the goods was a false declaration and that the appellant had not made a false declaration of his intention was not correct. The words " a person " in section 10(B) of the Bombay Act are wide enough to include a registered dealer or anybody else. The appellant has not sold the castor Oil to a person in the course or export out of Indian territory and the sales are therefore exempted from tax, and the appellant is not entitled to any relief under article 19 of the Constitution of India.

The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. The appellant moved the magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. The Magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived was high and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellant. The order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which provides that the wife includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On behalf of the respondent it was contended that the appellant had not proved that she was not living separately by mutual consent. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. In the instant case, the appellant has not proved that he was living separately by consent. The respondent has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case, on the contrary, is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree. [80E F] 2. The provision of section 127(3) (b) of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 is a social purpose and the social justice necessitates that a divorced woman should not be driven to material and moral dereliction to seek sanctuary in the streets. [80G] 3. The provision in section 127(1) (b), (3) (a) (b)(ii) and (iii) of the Cr. P.C. 1973 is a penal provision and must be strictly construed. The court must construe the provision in such a way as to advance the legislative intent and further the purpose of the provision. [81B C] 4. The provision is a social and beneficial provision and must receive a liberal construction. The court should not adopt an approach which would defeat the provision. The court is not empowered to add or to delete any word not found in the statute. [81D] 5. The court has to read the provision in the context of the social context and the legislative purpose. The court cannot rewrite, recast or reframe the legislation for the reason that it has no power to legislate. The court only interprets the law and cannot legislate it. [81E] 6. The court does not legislate. The Court only interprets it. The court interprets the legislation as it is and not legislate. [81F] 7. The court while interpreting a social legislation must not adopt an interpretation which would lead to absurdity or give rise to practical inconvenience or defeat the purpose of legislation. [82A] 8. The court, while interpreting a provision of a social welfare legislation, must not adopt a construction which would lead the legislation to some extent to a futility or to a efficacy either of the legislation or of the social philosophy of the legislation. [81G] 9. The court will not supply words which are not to be found in the legislation. The court can supply words which appear to be in the context in which the words are used. [82H] 10. The court may supply words which may appear to be rather vague or convey a meaning which may be obscure. [82G] 11. The court would not supply words in a statute which are not there. [82B] 12. The court in interpreting a social welfare statute should not adopt a technical approach. The court shall interpret the law as it is. [82C] 13. The court 's approach should be to give effect to the legislative intention and purpose of the legislation and not to make a new one. [82D] 14. The court interpreted the provision in a particular way. The court did not legislate. It is a court of law. [82E] 15. The court was not empowered to supply words which were not there. The court could supply words which appeared to be in its context. [82F] 16. The court held that the provision in section 125(3) of the 1973 Code is a penal one and must be construed strictly. The court said that the provision is a penal section and must be interpreted strictly. The Court said that the court should not resort to any technical approach. [82GH] 17. The court also held that the court cannot supply words which have been used in the legislation and the court can supply the words which appear in the legislation as a whole. [82CD] 18. The court further held that the Court cannot supply words in the legislation which are not found in it. [82DE] 19. The court directed the Magistrate to dispose of the case in accordance with law. [83A]

The appellant bid for Rs.11,900 for a shop in an auction held on 27.3.1988. He was given the shop. The name of the appellant was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector. The appellant did not deposit the amount. The name was placed in black list for the next year. The appellant challenged the order of black listing the appellant by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court set aside the order of the Collector. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The order of blackging of the appellant 's shop cannot be sustained. The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appellant in respect of future contracts, cannot be sustained in law. [867D] PG NO 869 PG NO 870 The order directing black listing of appellant 's bid in respect of the future contracts cannot be sustained, as it is not affected. [868B]

The respondent filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the basis of the fair rents fixed by the Rent Controller. The Rent Controller passed an order of eviction against the respondent. The respondent filed an appeal before the District Judge. The appeal was dismissed. The respondent then filed a revision petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The respondent thereafter filed a suit in the Civil Court for a declaration that the order of the Rent Controller was ultra vires in that no notice to quit had been given as required by law. The Civil Court dismissed the suit. The respondent thereupon filed a suit to recover arrears of rent. The suit was decreed. The respondent 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to decide the question of title. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Rent Controller does not have the jurisdiction to decide questions of title. It cannot be described as a matter that is squarely and directly in issue in the proceedings to which any finality can be attached, as the Rent Control ler by deciding the issue wrongly, cannot clothe himself with jurisdiction where none exists. All that the Rent Control Court has to do is to satisfy itself that the person seeking eviction or fixation of fair rent is a "landlord" who has prima facie, the right to receive the rents of the property in question. That the Rent Controller 's jurisdiction on this issue is limited is clear from the proviso to section 10(1) of the Act. So also, in an application under section 4, the jurisdiction of the Rent Controller is to determine a fair or standard rent for the premises. He has also no doubt to satisfy himself as to the extent of the premises qua which the relationship of landlord and tenant exists and in respect of which rent is receivable or payable. It is important to remember that when an owner files a suit for arrears of rent, it is open to the tenant, under the general law, to plead that no rent is payable in respect of the premises as, indeed, it belongs to him. [565H; 566A C] (2) The Rent Control l Court has no doubt to decide whether the relationship of the landlord and tenant existed. But it is not open to one of the parties to contend that the decision given by the Court of Small Causes, which has become final between the parties, is a total nullity which can be completely ignored. It is not open for one of the par ties to contend that a decision given by a Court of Small causes which has become finality between the parties is a nullity. The petitioner, a Forester in the State of Mysore, was given in the final integration list a position to which he objected. The petitioner, who was a respondent in the writ petition, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution of India, challenging the final list. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The petitioner had ample opportunity to make a representation against the preliminary list published. The petitioner had full opportunity to do that. The principle recognised in Shankariah 's case was not applicable to such a case. The petitioner was entitled to an opportunity to make representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the final gradation list was published. [829 C] The petitioner had a right to represent against the final gradation List. The petitioner could not have a grievance against the final list, if he had not been heard. [830 C] The principle recognised by Shankariah ' case was not attracted to the case. The High Courts had no power to interfere with the final gradation lists. [828 D] The petitioner was not entitled to a further opportunity to make his representation against the final seniority list. [831 A] Union of India vs G.M. Shankariah & Ors. ; , referred to. The petitioner 's contention that he was not heard after the final list was prepared, was not correct. The petitioner did not have a right to have a representation against a final gradation list. [881 C] The Court could not go into the merits of the case or otherwise of equation of posts which was a matter within the province of the Central Government. [882 C] The Central Government had to determine the equation of the posts and prepare a common gradation list by integration of services. To assist it in the task of equation, the Central Government was empowered to establish Advisory Committees. The Central Government was bound to ensure a fair and equitable treatment to officers in the matter of integration of services and preparation of gradation lists. It had also to give a proper consideration to the representations. [883 C] The power of the Courts is only to see that an authority has acted properly in accordance with the statute. If that is established, the decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous considerations, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [884 C]

The petitioners, who were granted Additional Licences under the Import Policy 1978 79 and the Import Policy 1988 91, applied for registration as Export Houses and for grant of Export House Certificate. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that the petitioners had failed to diversify their export of "other products" during the year 1977 78. The petitioners filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the said order of rejection. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. The petitioners have filed these appeals by special leave against the said orders of the High Court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners have failed to make out a case for interference by this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. [240E] 1.2 The petitioners have not made out a case that the Additional Licences granted to them under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 have to be treated at par with the Export Houses who are granted Additional Licenses under the Import and Export Policy for the subsequent years and since there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para (4) of para 215 in respect of Additional Licences issued to Export Houses under the Import Export Policy 1988 91 the petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation. [240F G] 1.3 The petitioners cannot claim the benefit of the same relaxation and assail the validity of sub para (10) of para 218 of the Import & Exports Policy 1988 91. [240G] Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers, ; ; Union of India & Ors. vs M/s. Indo Afghan Chambers of Commerce, ; ; D. Navinchandra & Co. vs Union of India, ; ; Indo Afghan Chamber of Commerce vs Union of lndia, ; ; Raj Prakash Chemicals Ltd. vs Union, ; ; M/s Indo Afghan Industries vs Union of india, ; and Indo Afghan Agencies Ltd. vs Chief Controller of Imports & Exports, ; , referred to. 2.1 The Additional Licences which are granted to the petitioners would be permissible if the import policy prevailing at the time of import permits them to import items falling under such category. This was also viewed in that light in the case of Indo Afghan Corporation vs Union ofIndia, ; and in the case the petitioners have been subjected to arbitrary and hostile discrimination. [240B C] 2.2 The High Court was right in holding that the petitioners have failed in making out a case of discrimination and that the Additional licences issued to the petitioners have to be extended to the petitioners. [240D] 3.1 The High Court has not laid down that canalisation could be ignored. High public policy, it must be emphasised, It involved in the scheme of canalisation. Although generally these are importable through public section agencies, it is permissible for any import policy to provide an exception to the rule and to declare that an importer might import a canalised item directly. They would be entitled to import items which were canalised or not if the import Policy prevailing at the date of import permitted them to import such items. This was not to say that canalised items could be imported directly by the importers ignoring the canalisation process. [240H; 241A] 3.2 The Additional Licenses issued to the petitioner have expired in the meanwhile. The petitioners cannot be said to be persons similarly circumstanced as Export Houses who have been granted Additional Licents under the Import Trade Policy 1978 79. The petitioners, therefore, cannot claim the benefits of the same concession and assail the valid validity of sub paras (10) and (10A) of para218 of the Import and Exports Policy 198891. [241B C] 3.3 The High Court, therefore, was right in rejecting the writ petitions filed by the petitioners. The writ petitions are dismissed. [241D] Union of indian vs Rajnikanth Bros., ; ; Union Carbide India Ltd. vs The Union of India; , ; ; D Navinchandra & Company vs Union of Indian, ; ; ; Indo Afghan Chambers of commerce vs Union of India, ; , distinguished. 3.4 The petitioners have also failed to make the necessary out come of the decision of the High Courts. The Additional Licents issued to the Petitioners have expired in their meanwhile. The writ petition is dismissed. [242B]

The appellant, a manufacturer of drums, was selling the drums in drums supplied by the buyer. The drums were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value of the drums could not be included in the assessable value of the goods. The Assistant Collector included the value of drums in the assessable proce dure. The Tribunal held that the appellant had not collected any amount in excess of the amount indicated in the price lists. The Tribunal, however, held that the cost of packing could be included in assessable value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the assessee. The appellant contended that the cost was not includible in the assessable vale of drums. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The cost of packing envisaged in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act for determining the "value" in relation to any excisable goods is only the "cost of such packing" incurred by the manufacturer and recovered from the buyer except where the packing is of a durable nature and is returnable by the buyers to the manufacturer. The "cost of packing" referred in section 4 (4)(d) (i) does not in clude within its ambit the cost of the packing not incurred by the manufacture when the packing was supplied by the buyers and not the manufacturer. This construction of the expression "cost of the packing" in section 4 of the Act clearly excludes in these matters the question of its addition to the price of goods recovered by the manufacturer from the buyer for determining the value in relation to the excisable goods for computing the duty payable on it. [9D E] 2. The cost envisaged in section 9(4)(b)(i) is only the normal price for which the goods are sold at the factory gate. An addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the prin ciple of price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. If the manufacturer supplies the drums and charges the customers separately therefore, then under section 4(1)(b)(ii) the cost of drums to the buyer has to be added to the price except where the cost of such packing is of durable nature and returnable to the buyer. [9E F] 3. The cost for packing envisaged in Section 4(4) (d)(i), does not in elude within its purview the cost of " packing not incurred" by the manufacturer when the packing supplied by the customer and not the assessee. This construction is of the express ing limited to the question of cost of packing in section 4. [9G H] 4. The cost is only the cost of those packing which is incurred by the assessee and recovered from its buyer. The cost referred to in section 4 is only the 'cost of such pack ing ' incurred by the appellant and recovered from it. [10A B] 5. The cost under section 4 (1) (b) (i), is only the actual cost to the manufacturer and not the cost to the buyer, and the cost of ' packing ' referred to in Section 4 (4) (b)(ii), is only that which is incurred and not the actual cost. [10B C] 6. The cost mentioned in section 4 has to be read as a whole and not separately. [10C] 7. The cost contemplated in section 4, (4) is only that degree of secondary packing which is necessary for the assessable article to be in the condition in which it is generally sold in the wholesale market at the factorygate. [10D] 8. The cost to the assessee of packing the drums in the drums is not includible in its assessable value. [10E] 9. The cost, of packing envisaged under section 4, is only the packing which was incurred by the appel lant and recovered from and is not the cost of any other packing which is not incurred by it. [11B] 10. The cost in section 4 includes the cost of secondary packing. [11C] 11. The cost has to be determined by the terms of section 4. The expression "cost" in section 9 (4) has to be understood in its ordinary sense. The cost may include the cost of materials and charges of packing or of packing, of containers and other materials and charges for and incidental to, the packing or transportation of the goods up to the stage of such packing. [12A B] 12. The cost which is referred to in the section is only that portion of the cost which is incurred in the factory by the assessee in respect of the goods sold. The cost can include only that portion which is incurred on the goods by the assessee himself. [12B C] 13. The cost incurred by the buyer in relation to goods which are not sold by the assessee is not includible. [12C] 14. The cost described in section 4 cannot be the cost of goods which are sold by the manufacturer. [12D] 15. The cost must be the "value", which under section 4 of Act, must include the cost price and the manufacturing cost. [12E] 16. The cost should be the "whole" or "part" of the cost. [13F] 17. The cost includes not only the cost but also the cost of insurance. [13G] 18. The cost specified in section 4 must be the cost which the manufacturer must pay to the manufacturer for the goods. [13H] 19. The cost and the cost are not only to be included in determining the value of excisable goods but also in determining the excise duty payable on the goods. It is only that amount which represents the cost of manufacture which is includible in the value of goods. [14A B] 20. The cost cannot include the cost which consists of the price of the goods for the goods and the cost relating to the manufacture of the goods which are only indirectly referred to in clause (a) of section 4(2). [14B] 21. The cost as defined in section 4 means the "value of the excisable goods" and includes the cost relating, to the manufacture. [14C] 22. The cost means the "wholesale cash price" charged by the assessee for the goods, at the factory, where the goods are delivered at the time of removal, wholly or in part, from the factory or any other premises, or (in any other manner whatsoever), and the cost and includes, in addition, any such cost which is included in the price at which the goods may be sold, and includes in addition to such cost, any amount which a manufacturer is liable to pay, if the buyer of the goods is a related person and the buyer is a related persons. [14D E] 23. The cost would include not only the "whale cash price", but also the "whire value" of the goods and any cost relating to "accessories". [14E] 24. The cost will include not only such costs as are incurred by the manufacturers in respect of those goods but also the amount of profit which the manufacturer will have to offer to the manufacturer in respect of that goods. The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. PW 3, the Principal of the training school issued exhibit P 2 show cause notice to the appellant as to why his licence for running the canteen should not be cancelled. The appellant had taken food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued the practice before the notice was issued. The prosecution case was that the appellant thereafter sent for PW 1, informed him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of Rs. 100. On 21.10.75, the appellant was charged with the offence of demanding and accepting a bribe of a sum of Rs.100. The prosecution witnesses supported the case. PW 1 affirmed the fact that the appellant made the demand and had also received the amount on 22.10. 1975. The recovery of the currency notes from the appellant was not challenged. The plea of the appellant was that PW 1 had returned the amount due to him and there had been no demand for a bribe as there had been a no tice for PW 1. The trial court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the appel lant and recorded the conviction. Before the High Court the appellant contended that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant had not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 was insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there was no conclusive evi dence to hold that the appellant was guilty. The High Court took the view that the evidence of PW I find corroboration in the testimony of PW 2 and 6 and the contemporary records. The recovery was not challenged and the plea of appellant was that there was a consistent case even from the earliest opportunity that the currency notes found in his possession was the money returned by PW 1, the cir cumstances of the case would probabalise this case of the appellant and the presumption, if any, arising under section 4 was rebutted and the conviction could not therefore be sustained. The High court thought that though the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section 161. The appellant has reiterated the contentions before this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The presumption under section 4(1) of the Act is rebutted by the evidence of the prosecution witnesses. The appellant was not able to show that there had been consistent explanation for the appellant. The appellant did not even by preponderance of probability succeed in rebutting the presumption. The argument that clause (d) of section 5(1) is not attracted on the proved facts is also not impressive. [338B C] 2. The appellant is entitled to the benefit of doubt. The evidence of PW 3, Principal of the Training School, is not sufficient to hold that there had be en a valid demand for a sum of money. The evidence is not sufficient for holding that the appellant had demanded and accepted a sum of rupees 100 from PW 1. [338D E] 3. The appellant 's plea that PW 1 was not present at the time of the demand was not even suggested to PW 1. It cannot, therefore, be said that there had not been consistent explanation of the appellant. [338E] 4. The appellant having been convicted under section 161 IPC and section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corruption Ac t, the presumption under section 5(i)(d) of the said Act is rebutted. [338F] 5. The appellant cannot be convicted under section 5 (1) (d) read with section 5(ii) of the P.C. Act. [338G]

The petitioner was an officer of a company. He was in the employment of the company. He had been allotted a flat in the company 's project. The company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act, 1971. The Magistrate took cognizance of the complaint and directed issue of process. The first and foremost contention of the petitioner was that the provision contained in section 630 of the Act was a penal provision and, therefore, must be subject to a strict construction and there was no room for intendment. The High Court rejected the contention and held that the term 'officer or employee ' in sub section (1) of section 630 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and employees of a company but also to include past officers and employees who were in the employment at the time of their employment. The High court also held that the words 'any such property ' in section 630(l)(b) relate to property specified in cl. (a) viz. property of a company wrongfully taken possession of by a present officer or employee of the company, and that the words must be interpreted in furtherance of the object and purpose of the legislation which would suppress the mischief and advance the remedy. The Court, however, held that the expression 'any such Property ' in section 630(1) of the Act must be read as 'any property of a Company ' and not as 'any Property of a Company. The Court accordingly held that the provision in section 630 was not applicable to the present case. The Court also held that section 630 of Act was applicable only to the existing officers and employees and not to past officers and that the phrase 'any such ' in section 631(l)(a) must be read in the context of the words 'a past officer or employee '. The Court held that the phrase must be read with the words 'or any such property ' occurring in cl. 'a ' and 'b ' of section 630(1) and that the said phrase must be interpreted as 'any such properties ' as are specified in cl 'a '. The High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras have taken a view that the term "officer or employee" in sub section(1) must be interpreted strictly and that there is no room for implication. The Court has also held that sub section (2) of section 6 of the Act makes it an offence if an officer or employee who is in the employment when he is sought to be proceeded against, wrongfully retains or occupies the property of the company after the termination of his employment. The Court rejected the argument that section 630 is a penal provision. The Court observed that the legislature never intended to include past officer and employees of the company within the ambit of section 630 of The Act is a social welfare legislation intended to protect the employees from harassment and exploitation of the employer. The Court further held that the legislature intended to provide a summary procedure for retrieving the property of a public company and for the recovery of such property by the issue of process under sub section (3) of section 5 of the Act. The Court therefore held that the provisions of section 630 are not applicable to past officers or employees of a public limited company. The Court however held that the word 'officer ' in section 5(1) includes past officers and the words 'and the property of any company ' in section 30(1) include past officers. The Court negatived the contention that section 630 was a penal statute and that the legislature had deliberately used the words 'property of a company ' in the section. The Court found that the legislature did not intend to include past employees and officers of a company within the meaning of section 630. The Court dismissed the appeal of the petitioner. The petitioner filed a special leave petition in this Court against the decision of the Calcutta High Court. Dismissing the petition, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High courts of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay have taken a consistent view that the terms 'officer or employees ' in sub s.(1) of s.630 of the Act are to be interpreted strictly. The Court is unable to accept the contention that the legislature has deliberately used the word 'or ' in the sub section. [176G H] 2. The appellant was the Mahant of the Sansthan. The deity of his worship was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. In the Sanad granted by the Government of Bombay to the Sansthan, the Government recognised the Sansthan as a public religious endowment and only on that basis the grant was continued. The appellant filed an appeal under section 70 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, before the Charity Commissioner, Bombay, who by his order of August 25, 1956, affirmed the decision of the Assistant Charity Commissioner. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Sansthan was an endowment. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: (1) The Sansthan was a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. [528 D] (2) The appellant relied on all the documents for the purpose of showing that the endowment was private only because ownership of the donor was transferred to the donee. The reference to Sakharam Maharaj Sansthan, wherever it appears, is only for the purpose, of identification and commemoration of the hallowed saint who had admittedly founded the same. The principles of law for determination of the question whether an endowment is public or private are fairly well settled. While in the former the beneficiaries are persons who are ascertained or capable of being ascertained, in the latter they constitute a body which is incapable of ascertainment. In the former the beneficiary is a trustee, and in the latter, the trustee. [525 B C] (3) The appellant relies on all the above documents for the purposes of showing that endowment is private only because the ownership of the doner is transferred to the donor. The appellant relies upon the oral and documentary evidence to show that the Sansthan is a public trust. [526 B C] Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji vs Rannchhoddas Kalidas and Ors., ; ; State of Bihar & Ors. vs Sm. And in such circumstances proof of user by the public without interference would be cogent evidence that the dedication was in favour of the public. [527 B] (4) The appellant ' reliance on the oral evidence is not correct. The appellant relied upon the oral evidence of the Mahant and the Mahant himself. The Mahant himself was a celibate and the successive disciples who succeeded as adhikaris of the Gadi were also celibates. The Mahant and the successive followers of the deity are paid their cost of journey. The public is not allowed to go to the temple as the temple is meant for the Darshan by the public. The public are not allowed to enter the temple as a matter of right. The public may not be allowed to go inside the temple as they are not allowed access to the temple. The public also may not be permitted to go inside. The public, however, are not allowed entry to the temple and the public are allowed to worship in the temple. [529 C E] (5) The appellant has not been able to show that there is any evidence of dedication to the public or public user of the temple as of right. [530 A] (6) The appellant also relied on the oral and the documentary evidence to prove that the Sansthan and the temple are public religious endowments. The appellant also relies on the oral testimony of the Mahant himself to show that he has been in possession of the Sansthan and its management for over a century. [531 A B] (7) The appellant cannot be allowed to rely on the oral or documentary evidence to establish that the Sansthan has any independent right to the public. It is not always possible to have all the features of a public trust in a given case. Even some of the tests laid down by this Court may, in a given ease, be sufficient to enable the court to come to a conclusion about the character of the trust. [534 B C] In the instant case, the evidence shows that the Sansthan, which is a public temple, is a public one. The public have a right to worship in that temple as of any other place of worship. The public believe in the deity as a substitute for the private worship and worship. The deity is the substitute of the public deity. The public worship the deity in the temple as an independent deity. The deity installed in the temple is a public deity. [535 C D] (8) The appellant rely on the evidence of the Manager of the Sansthan to show that it is a public endowment. The Manager is a celibate and the deity installed in his temple is a substitute of the deity. The manager is a ceilbate and the deity is the substituted substitute of the idol. The public generally worship in the public temple. The deity has a right to enter the public temple if the public is entitled to enter it. The public has a right of entry into the temple if the deity is not entitled to enter the deity. [534 E G] (9) The appellant further relied on the evidence that the Sansthan had been in possession and management for over 50 years. The public believed in the deity in its original form and the public believe in its original manifestation. The public had a right to take part in the management of the deity as an independent and independent deity. [635 H] (10) The appellant had not been able able to show how the public have a independent right to enter into the Sansthan. [636 A] (11) The appellant is not entitled under the Act to rely on oral evidence to establish the public user of a public temple. [638 C] (12) The appellant did not produce any evidence of the public user. [639 C] (13) The appellant was not able to show any evidence of user by public without interference. [640 D] (14) The appellant could not be allowed in the circumstances of the case to rely on documentary evidence to support his case that the Sansthan in question was a public temple and not a private one. [641 E] (15) The appellant failed to show that any evidence was led by the public to show that public had a independent right of worship in the Sansthan. The petitioner was a defaulter in the payment of income tax and the Collector of Bombay issued a warrant of arrest against him under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, for the recovery of the amount certified under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The petitioner challenged the validity of the warrant on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that section 46(1) of the Act under which the Collector issued the warrant was void under article 13(1) as it was repugnant to article 14 of the Constitution, and (2) that section 13 of Bombay City Land revenue Act, 1876 under which the warrant of arrest was issued by the Additional Collector was void under articles 13(1), 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. Held, that section 46 (1) of Bombay City land Revenue Act, 1879, under which the Additional Collector of Bombay was empowered to issue a warrant of attachment and sale of the property of the petitioner, was void under the Constitution and was not void under article 19(1) (f) and article 31(1) and (2). The State of Bombay vs Narasu Appal Gondia, ; , referred to. The State of Bihar vs Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga, [1952] S.C.R. 889, distinguished. The State Of Bihar vs Maharajdhar Singh, [1952) S.C R. 889 and The State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, ; , relied on. The State vs Bamneshwar Singh, [1954] S. C. R. 803, distinguished. Held, further, that the procedure prescribed by section 13 of Bom. LVII of 1864 for the recovery Of arrears of land revenue was a procedure which was different from that prescribed by section 157 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, and the former was a procedure for the recovery by the Collector of the arrears of land Revenue and the latter was a procedure prescribed by the Bombay Land revenue Code, 1879. The State was not therefore entitled to challenge the validity of section 13 of Act LVII of 1876. The State had not been deprived of its property by the impugned Act and the petitioner was not entitled to any relief on the ground that the impugned Act was repugnant to articles 19(1), 31(1), 14 and 19(1). The State had also not been deprived by the impugned section of the right to recover arrears of land tax from the petitioner by virtue of the provisions of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1946, and the petitioner could not therefore be deprived of his property by the provisions of section 13 Of the Bombay City land revenue Act, 18 1876. The impugned Act was a law relating to land revenue and was not repugnant to article 19(i)(f) of the Constitu tion. The State could not be deprived of its land revenue by the impugned law under article 31(2) as it had not been reserved for the consideration of the President. The State Act was not repugnant under article 14 of Constitution. The State Legislature was competent to enact the impugned Act under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The impugned section 13 Of Bom. L VII of 1864 was not repugnant either to article 19 (1) (g) or article 31(a) of the constitution. The State Government was not therefore competent to issue the warrant of attachment under section 13 Of Bombay City Land ' Revenue Act, 1864, and the Collector had no jurisdiction to attach the property of a defaulter under section 13. The State having been deprived of the property by the Bombay Act LVII Of 1876, the petitioner could no longer be deprived of it by the impugned act. The State 's power to recover arrears was not affected by article 19(5) of the Consti tution. The State cannot be deprived of the right of the petitioner to recover arrears by the impugned legislation under article 19 (5) of Constitution. State of Bihar V. Maharajadhirjee Sir Kameshwar Prasad Singh, [1959] S.c.R. 729, referred to. Held, also, that the impugned section 13 of Maharashtra Act LVII, of 1864, was not repugnant tO article 14 of Indian Constitution and was valid. The State has not been deprived under article 31 (2) of its property and the petitioner cannot be deprived by the Act of his property under article 31 of the Constitution by the impugned enactment. The State is not therefore entitled under article 31 to challenge the Act on the ground of contravention of article 14 of India. The State can not be deprived by a law under article 19 of the Constitution of the right guaranteed by article 19 (6) of the same Constitution. The petitioner was not therefore, entitled to any of the reliefs claimed by him.

The appellant was a public limited company carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of textiles. It was a public company and its working hours were from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. The hours of work were 9 hours per day, 9 hours per week and 9 hours per hour. The work of the appellant was to provide a certain number of hours of work per day for the workmen. The hours were fixed by the appellant at 9 hours per shift. The work was to be done at the rate of 8 hours per day. The appellant fixed the hours of work at 9 hours and 9 hours a day. The workmen claimed that the hours of rest fixed at 9 hours were excessive and should be reduced to 3 hours per day and that the extra work beyond 9 hours per working day should be paid for at a higher rate. The appellant contended that the hours fixed at 9 were excessive and that the workmen should be paid at the higher rate. Held, that the hours were fixed at 9 and 9 hours each day and that there was no reason for the appellant to fix the extra hours at 9 hours each night. The working hours were 9 hours a week and 9 working hours per day respectively. The work in a day was to be carried on at 9 hours a month and 9 hours at 9 p.m., and the work in a week was to be at 9 hours. The work at 9 was to be completed at 9 p m. and 9 hours after 9 p. m. The work during the extra hours was to be of 9 hours a working day and 9 hours as a weekly day. The work for the extra hours consisted of 8 hours a day and 9 working days. The work up to 9 hours per morning was to be taken as the working day and the rest of the hours were to be taken in a day. In the former there was 3 hours ' overtime and in the latter there was 4 hours ' overtime. The work done at 9 hours was to the extent of 8 hours and 9 working day. The working of the appellant company was to be 9 hours per month and 9 working working day per day respectively and the rest was to be 4 hours per day per day. In a 12 hour shift the 9 hours work was to include 8 hours a week. The work beyond 9 was to include 4 hours a day, 9 working days and 9 working 30 days. The working time of the appellant for the extra work was 9 hours a work day and 9 days a week respectively. The extra work beyond the 9 hours per work day was to include the 8 hours a work of 9 hours per a day. It was not a period of more inaction because there was no work for him. The appellant was entitled to fix the hours of working at 9 hours on any day and to fix the rest of hours at 9. The working day of the appellant 's company was 9 hours per year and 9 hours on a week day. The extra hours were to include 8 working hours a day while the rest of 9 hours were to take place at 9 hours every day. The hours fixed at the 9 hours were 9 working days, 9 working working days and 8 working hours. The working days of the appellant were 9 hours and 8 hours a month. The extra ordinary work of the workmen was to be paid for 8 hours a working hour and 9 hours an hour. The extra hour was to be calculated at the rate applicable to a working day. In calculating the extra hours the extra hour was not to be included. The working hour was to include both the hours of 9 hours and the rest. The working was to be spread over at 9 hours, 9 hours a year and 9 working hour per day. There was no reason why the extra hours should be taken at 9 hours for the purpose of calculating the extra hour. The working in a 12 hour ' shift was to be 10 hours a day or 9 hours a weekly day and 9 or 10 hours a week respectively, and the rest for the extra hour consisted of 8 working hours per week. The working and the extra hours were not to be taken into account in calculating the extra working hours.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court set aside the conclusion of the trial court. The main ground which was before the High Court was as to whether the provisions of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 will be applicable to these proceedings in view of the fact that although the premises were let out in June 1976 but as the assessment was made on October 1, 1976 the provisions of the Act referred to above will not apply for 10 years from October 1,1976 and therefore the suit could be decreed as the protection available under this Act will not be available to the tenant. The High court after discussing various decisions came to the conclusion that in view of language of Section 2(2) of the Act it could not be doubted that period of 10 years will commence from the date of assessment i.e. October 1,76 that it is in that view of the matter that the High Court decreed the suit and hence the present appeal. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was not pending on the date on which the Act came into force. An attempt was made to contend that so far as the present property is concerned the Act will be deemed to have come into force on the expiry of 10 years i.e., 1.10.86 but this contention could not be accepted as it is very clear from the language of Section 39 of the Act that it applied only to a suit pending on the day of commencement of the Act i.e 15.7.72 and this is the view taken in the Om Prakash Gupta 's case wherein it was observed: "The appellant in the present case only seeks the protection of the new Rent Act which became applicable to the premises in question during the pendency of the litigation. The Court observed that if during the pendency the proceedings 10 years have elapsed the tenant is entitled to the protection under the Act and in coming to this conclusion the Court considered the language of section 39 of the new Act and it observed: "the appellant in the instant case only seeks protection of the newly constructed building the provisions of this Act will be of no avail. Section 20 of the new rent Act provides a bar to a suit for ejectment of a tenant except on the specified grounds as provided in the section. Sub section (4) of section 20 stipulated that in any suit for eviction on the grounds mentioned in cl. (a) to sub section (2) viz. the arrears of rent, if at the first hearing of the suit the tenant in default pays all arrears of rent to the landlord or deposits in court the entire amount of rent and damages for the use and occupation of the building due from him, such damages for use and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the landlord 's cost of the suit in respect thereof after deducting therefrom any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section (1) of section 30, the court may, in lieu of passing a decree for eviction on that ground, pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction onthat ground. Section 39 of this Act indicates that the benefit of new Act will be given to the tenant if the conditions contemplated in those sections are satisfied. Section 39 also indicates that the parties are entitled to make necessary amendment in their pleadings and to adduce additional evidence where necessary. " But unfortunately attention of the Court was not drawn to the Om Prakash 's case which specifically considered this Act and the language of s.39 in particular and was a decision of a Bench of three Judges which is binding on this Court. The restriction on the right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in this Act under section 20 and the language is also significant. Keeping in view the language of this section if we examine the provisions contained in sub section (3) of section 2 it will be clear that for a newly constructed building, the provisions of that Act will not apply. For a newly constructed Building the provisions of section 20 can not be attracted and therefore it is clear that during the pendency or 10 years expired the restriction will not be attracted as the suit has been instituted within 10 years and therefore restriction as provided for in section 20 can no be attracted. [166E H; 167A B] 1.2 The appellant tenant could not be given the advantage of the provisions contained ' in this Act. In this view of the mater the appeal is without any substance and is dismissed. The appellant was a lessee of a large area of land in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period of five years. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease. The Collector passed an order on December 27, 1955, declaring that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was for the period exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the order of the Collector. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant came up in appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave. The appellant contended that the order of termination of the lease was invalid as the Government had not formed the necessary satisfaction as required by the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. Held, that the order was valid. The words " such right " in the third proviso to section 2(1) refer to the rights created on or after July 1, 1948, and the third proviso does not govern the second proviso. The words of the second proviso relate to the rights mentioned in the second proviso, that is to say, rights created on and after July 1. 1945. The scheme of section 20 of the Abolition is to provide, firstly, that rights created by way of lease or otherwise by the landholder prior to the notified date should be deemed to be valid and all rights and obligations arising thereunder on or after the notified date were to be enforceable by or against the Government; secondly, that the rights created before the notified date, but after July 1 1945, for a period exceeding one years would not be enforceable against the government. Thirdly, that the Government must do some overt act to terminate the transaction. The machinery for such termination is to be found in the third provi sion. The third proviso does nothing more than add some terms to the lease. When, however, the lease is determined under the second proviso these terms must also fall with it. The words in the third provision are not intended to be used for the sake of the Government but for the purpose of the Government. In the present case, the Government had formed the necessary opinion that it was in the public interest to terminate the lease and that the Government had done so. The third provi so deals with the termination of rights created before July 1, 1949, and the second proviso deals with the right created after July 1., 1945.
